58/**
59 * `sync_io`-pattern counterpart to async-I/O-pattern transport::struc::Channel.
60 *
61 * @see transport::struc::Channel and util::sync_io doc headers. The latter describes the general pattern which
62 * we implement here; it also contrasts it with the async-I/O pattern, which the former implements.
63 * Which of the two to use depends on your needs, as summarized in the util::sync_io doc header.
64 *
65 * All notes on functionality in transport::struc::Channel (a/k/a alias Channel::Async_io_obj) doc
66 * header apply to us. The difference, as usual given `sync_io` and async-I/O mutual counterparts, is in how
67 * results are reported. Because struc::Channel in general stands apart from the many concept impls
68 * of `Blob_sender`, `Blob_receiver`, etc. -- e.g., Native_socket_stream -- it may be helpful to summarize
69 * how this `sync_io`-pattern type reports results. The APIs look somewhat different from those
70 * core-layer guys owing to the more complex mission statement here versus there.
71 *
72 * - `expect_*(..., F)`: This says you want messages of a certain type, and when one arrives to invoke `F(I)`,
73 * `I` being the in-message. However, depending on the API 1+ message(s) may already have been cached and
74 * are immediately available. These are synchronously emitted via an out-arg; for example expect_msgs() takes
75 * a list-of-in-messages out-arg. Depending on the API future messages may be relevant and will be emitted
76 * via `F()`.
77 * - `async_request(&M, ..., F)`: This says you want `M` sent and expect 1 or 0+ (depending on args) response(s),
78 * and when one arrives to invoke `F(I)`, `I` being a response. Since it is not possible to have received a
79 * response to a not-yet-sent out-message, that is just how it works. There are no synchronous out-args.
80 * - `set_*unexpected_response_handler()`: If it's set, and an unexpected-response event occurs, this fires.
81 * If not, it doesn't. There are no synchronous out-args.
82 * - `start_and_poll(F)`: This begins incoming-direction operation. `F()` is the on-error handler. It fires
83 * up to once per `*this` to indicate underlying `Owned_channel` or other channel-hosing error (including
84 * receiving graceful-close). An error may synchronously occur right then, plus any `expect_*()`- and
85 * `async_request()`-triggered in-messages may be synchronously detected. Therefore -- and this is quite
86 * rare (singular as of this writing in Flow-IPC):
87 * - `start_and_poll(F)` may *synchronously* (!) call a number of queued-up (in a sense) handlers including:
88 * - `expect_*()` handlers;
89 * - `async_request()` handlers;
90 * - `set_*unexpected_response_handler()` handlers;
91 * - on-error handler `F()` itself.
92 *
93 * (One more exception of the same kind: expect_log_in_request() can, in one corner case, synchronously invoke
94 * the on-error handler; see its doc header. By far most users will never deal with log-in -- ipc::session does
95 * it internally on an internal-use `Channel` -- and therefore will never call expect_log_in_request().)
96 *
97 * Tip: If you'd rather not worry about `start_and_poll()`-executed handlers -- except on-error handler which
98 * might occur regardless -- then avoid calling `expect_*()`, async_request(), `set_*()` before
99 * start_and_poll(). (No in-messages are ever dropped, so you won't "miss" something by registering an
100 * expectation too late.) That said there's nothing wrong per se with setting those things up before
101 * start_and_poll() either. Just be ready for the `_and_poll` part.
102 *
103 * ### Thread safety ###
104 * The thread safety notes in transport::struc::Channel (a/k/a alias Channel::Async_io_obj) doc
105 * header do not apply here. (If you're familiar with the `sync_io` pattern, this probably won't surprise you.)
106 * To wit, given one particular `*this`:
107 * - The `const` accessors struct_builder_config(), struct_lender_session(), struct_reader_config(),
108 * owned_channel(), owned_channel_mutable() and key utility create_msg()
109 * are always safe to call concurrently with any other ops.
110 * - Now consider the remaining methods plus any `on_active_ev_func()` passed to the function you furnished via
111 * `this->start_ops()`:
112 * - You may not call any 2+ operations from this set concurrently.
113 *
114 * @internal
115 * ### Implementation overview ###
116 * Like all `sync_io`-core object types, this one is essentially a linear state machine with no
117 * actual asynchronicity or concurrency. (Some `sync_io`s do need to start threads in order to perform
118 * unavoidable blocking operations -- namely the `Blob_stream_mq_*` guys with at least the bipc MQ type which
119 * lacks an FD-tickling API -- but this can be thought of similarly to a background kernel service. Anyway
120 * sync_io::Channel doesn't even feature that caveat.)
121 *
122 * So as with other `sync_io` cores, it's a linear sequence of API calls into `*this` that may not be
123 * mutually concurrent (when non-`const`). As with those others in this context an API call is either a
124 * method call (duh) or an async-wait `Event_wait_func` calling into `*this` via `(*on_active_ev_func)()`.
125 * Hence we don't care what thread a given thing runs in, as long as our user (e.g., transport::struc::Channel)
126 * doesn't invoke things concurrently.
127 *
128 * So it's "just" a matter of implementing each direction -- outgoing (send() et al), incoming
129 * (`expect_*()`, async_request()), and their (reasonably limited) interplay (e.g., async_request() conceptually =
130 * a send() + registering expectation of particular future response in-message(s)).
131 *
132 * ### Implementation: layers ###
133 *
134 * #### Outgoing direction ####
135 * In the outgoing direction, the layers involved are fairly straightforward: send() is synchronous. When it is
136 * called, the zero-copy serialization of the structured out-message #Msg_out has been completed: the raw blobs
137 * comprised by it are easily accessible from the #Msg_out (Msg_out_impl::emit_serialization()) passed to send()
138 * (as is the optional #Native_handle). The 1+ blobs + the #Native_handle are synchronously `Channel::send_*()`ed,
139 * and then send() returns. In addition, but still synchronously within send(), each such user message obj internally
140 * contains another similarly-serialized message: the *metadata* message. (For performance it is stored as a header
141 * therein.) This message, with a schema in `structured_msg.capnp` (a detail/
142 * file), represents a *description* of the daddy #Msg_out. Its schema
143 * is controlled by us and is sufficiently small to require just one segment (blob) and no #Native_handle.
144 * This contains information about the message (a/k/a metadata), notably: its message ID (discussed below),
145 * the ID of the message to which it responds (or 0 if unsolicited), and the session token. (For perf this header
146 * is contained in the same memory buffer as the first, and often only, capnp-segment of the user message.)
147 * To summarize, then, send() of a user message in fact sends exactly 1 metadata message/header within
148 * a blob that also stores segment 1 of the user messages, plus 0+ blobs (segments)
149 * serializing the rest of the user message. (async_request() = internally such a send() more or less, plus registering
150 * that future in-message(s) with certain metadata content are expected.)
151 *
152 * Lastly, for some special purposes, we sometimes send internal messages. An internal message consists of
153 * *only* the metadata; hence we just generate that same thing directly into a little blob, fill out the
154 * optional internal-message-body field; and that fact indicates there is no user message (no segment 1, no anything)
155 * to also scan. Hence in this case exactly 1 `Blob` (segment) is sent, as for a typical (1-segment)
156 * user message but without the actual user message.
157 *
158 * In the few cases where an internal message is required, internal code calls send_core() directly, passing a
159 * 1-`vector` of `Blob_const`s. Note that no #Msg_out is involved at all.
160 *
161 * As for a user message, it goes through send() or async_request() each of which
162 * invokes send_impl() (for the actual sending part). That guy converts a #Msg_out (facaded-into a Msg_out_impl,
163 * to get at its internal representation which is `private` to the user) into an N-`vector` (where N is 1+)
164 * of `Blob_const`s. Then send_core() takes those and sends them out.
165 *
166 * #### Incoming direction ####
167 * In the incoming direction, it is much more complex. Receiving a blob, or blob+handle pair, is by definition
168 * a (potentially) asynchronous operation; and a given structured in-message may consist of more than 1 blob/blob+handle
169 * pair. The zero-copy deserialization invoked by the user can only occur once all of them are received, so
170 * we must build up 1 given structured in-message over 1+ single-message async-read ops and only emit the result
171 * (a newly allocated/cted Msg_in a/k/a #Msg_in_ptr) to the user once the last of the 1+ async-read ops
172 * finishes. So that's 2 layers: async-read op at the #Owned_channel level; then the structured level once a
173 * Msg_in is ready. Msg_in represents, conceptually, a pointer to 1-2 serialized
174 * in-messages: the metadata in-message (always present) and, except for internal messages, the user-supplied
175 * in-message (supplied originally via #Msg_out). However, to the user, only the latter is accessible,
176 * and an internal message is by definition never emitted to the user (if it were, there would be nothing for them
177 * to access). We access the mdt-stuff of a #Msg_in via the Msg_in_impl facade.
178 *
179 * @note Detour: Batch-receiving! Please see concept class transport::Native_handle_receiver doc header first,
180 * then come back here. In short, batch-receiving is the activity of making 1 `transport::Channel`-layer
181 * `.async_receive_*_batch()` call to "simultaneously" (ideally with 1 OS-call, using a reused
182 * Msg_batch_in object) receiving potentially-many unstructured in-messages. We use this, because we want
183 * to be fast. (The max size of the batch = `Msg_in_pipe::S_RCV_BATCH_SIZE`; e.g., 64 or 1; this # comes from
184 * `Owned_channel::S_RCV_NATIVE_HANDLE_BATCH_SZ_RECOMMENDATION` or
185 * `Owned_channel::S_RCV_BLOB_BATCH_SZ_RECOMMENDATION` depending on the
186 * pipe in question.) Now, this code path would work perfectly well even if it is 1. However, we do have a
187 * code-path specifically tailored to unbatched-receiving, and we've left this code-path in because (1) it was
188 * available, and (2) perf here is very important (we know from profiling experience). So
189 * `if constexpr(RCV_BATCH_SIZE == 1)`, we always invoke that code-path; otherwise the other code-path. In either
190 * case a Msg_batch_in is still used (so, of capacity 1 in one of the two cases), but with 1-batches it is an
191 * extremely simple Generic_msg_batch_in, and the non-batching code-path just always targets its slot 0, using
192 * none of the other features of the Msg_batch_in concept (not even Msg_batch_in::n_used() which remains 0).
193 *
194 * The preceding non-detour paragraph talks only of *one* Channel pipe. It is possible #Owned_channel contains 2 pipes
195 * (Channel::S_HAS_2_PIPES), operating potentially in parallel. (This may be useful for perf; discussion omitted
196 * here.) Naturally this creates the possibility of reordering of in-messages. Hence, optionally, there is
197 * another layer between completing a Msg_in (#Msg_in_ptr) and emitting it: a simple reassembly queue.
198 * To make this work: each in-message (hence each out-message instance) is supplied with a unique message ID
199 * (required anyway for, at least, request-response correlation); and that message ID doubles as a *sequence #*
200 * (1, 2, ...). #Reassembly_q is a reassembly queue that is (probably infrequently) used to temporarily
201 * store out-of-order structured in-messages, flushing them once the gap between last-emitted-to-next-layer
202 * in-message-sequence-# and lowest-in-message-sequence-#-in-reassembly-queue is filled.
203 *
204 * Okay; let's assume an in-message has gone through the above 2-3 layers (Channel layer, (optional) reassembly
205 * queue layer, Msg_in completion layer). Can we finally emit it to the user? Often yes... but generally
206 * no:
207 *
208 * In the incoming-direction, we add *notification* and *response* expectation APIs (these are
209 * mandatory before the `*this` user receives an emitted in-message via handler). This adds a further layer
210 * of processing. Once a Msg_in (#Msg_in_ptr) is assembled and ready to deserialize, one of 2 things
211 * happens: either an expect_msg() or async_request() has registered a handler for this in-message -- then it
212 * is immediately emitted to that handler (done!); or not -- then it is stored inside `*this`. (Once a handler
213 * is *subsequently* registered, the appropriate stored in-messages shall be emitted via synchronous out-args
214 * such as `qd_msgs` for expect_msgs().)
215 *
216 * That's the overview. Various doc headers on `private` types and/or data members should fill in the details.
217 *
218 * ### Protocol negotiation ###
219 * A good place to familiarize oneself with this topic is a similar section in the doc header of a core-layer
220 * (lower level) facility; sync_io::Native_socket_stream_impl is probably best, but sync_io::Blob_stream_mq_sender_impl
221 * and sync_io::Blob_stream_mq_receiver_impl are similar (albeit split up, because an MQ is unidirectional).
222 * We urge you to be comfortable with that before reading on, as a certain facility with the subject matter is
223 * needed for the following discussion.
224 *
225 * Consider the big picture: transport::Channel (unstructured), over which a `*this` operates, is composed of those
226 * lower-level transports, namely Blob_sender, Blob_receiver, etc., impls bundled in a certain way. We sit at the
227 * next-higher layer (structured layer). We operate a protocol (multiple cooperating protocols actually) on top
228 * of the protocol(s) at that unstructured layer, and that protocol can evolve (gain versions) over time too.
229 * The question is how to arrange forward-compatible (in some sense) protocol negotiation at this higher layer.
230 *
231 * One approach would be to not add independent protocol versioning/negotiation at our layer at all and simply rely
232 * on that work done already at the aforementioned unstructured (lower) layer. Certainly that would mean less code
233 * for us and a bit of perf/reponsiveness gain from not adding more negotiation traffic (that part not being super
234 * significant, as this is all only at the start of a channel's lifetime). The negative shows up in the scenario
235 * where the low-level protocol needs no change, but our higher-level protocol does. Now we have to bump up the
236 * version for the lower layer, explaining this is only to support differences at unrelated higher layers.
237 * (Formally speaking the lower-layer APIs can be used without us at all, and there are surely use cases for that.)
238 * Moreover -- we don't often talk about this outside the top-level common.hpp -- but the `ipc_core` module
239 * is (as of this writing) a separate library from ours, `ipc_transport_structured`; so one would need to change the
240 * code in a different library, release it, etc., despite no other behavior changes in that library. That's not great.
241 *
242 * So we've decided to keep it clean (if more complex and involving more code and designing) and have each layer do its
243 * own negotiation.
244 *
245 * Well, no problem. Having read about this as recommended above, you'll know it's just a matter of keeping a
246 * Protocol_negotiator object in a `*this` and sending and receiving a message/payload before any other message/payload.
247 * As of this writing there *is* only the initial version of the protocol (1), so we don't yet need to worry about
248 * potential backward-compatibility/knowing which version to actually speak from a range of 2 or more; etc.
249 *
250 * Update: we have made changes and now are at protocol version V (for simplicity, across the board... the "board" of
251 * which I speak is about to be described). For simplicity we speak only that version; there
252 * is no backward-compatibility with version-1-speaking software.
253 * (V is #S_PROTOCOL_VERSION_MIN and #S_PROTOCOL_VERSION_MAX.)
254 *
255 * That said, the challenge here is more subtle than that. Sure, we can negotiate *a* version at this layer, no
256 * problem. The problem: there are *multiple* protocols operating at this layer. There are at least two:
257 * -# How do blob/handle pairs transmitted over the transport::Channel translated into structured capnp messages?
258 * This even depends on template params `Builder_config_t` and `Reader_config_t`: As of this writing
259 * there are at least:
260 * - Heap_fixed_builder + Heap_reader: Heap-based arrangement, wherein all messages are transmitted directly
261 * (via copy) as blobs going through the unstructured `Channel`: The lead message blob is a capnp
262 * `struct StructuredMessage`, potentially followed by N (where N >= 1 and is communicated via
263 * that `StructuredMessage`) blobs, each representing a capnp-segment, those segments together making up
264 * a user message's serialization.
265 * - shm::Builder + shm::Reader: SHM-based arrangement, wherein all messages are transmitted
266 * as tiny SHM-handle-only-storing blobs, and then on the receiving side each such SHM-handle is taken
267 * to point to a list-of-capnp-segments (living in SHM), those segments together making up a
268 * user message's serialization. (Hence end-to-end zero-copy, only the SHM-handles actually transmitted
269 * via the underlying unstructured `Channel`.)
270 * - HOWEVER!!! Since the aforementioned metadata `StructuredMessage` is tiny (and of capped size), it is still
271 * (as with the heap-based arrangement) directly inside the (only, in the SHM case) blob transmitted via IPC.
272 * It is again the header; and for user messages after the header comes the encoding of the SHM-handle
273 * (pointing to a list-of-capnp-segments). This was an important optimization actually; historically we
274 * used to transmit the mdt-`StructuredMessage` as a totally separate in-SHM thing; this did all kinds of
275 * ultimately costly stuff including unneeded heap-allocations.
276 * -# The capnp messages aren't just user messages either; internally we have internal messages and, more
277 * importantly, the metadata-bearing leading messages containing key stuff like the message ID,
278 * notification/response info, etc. The (internally used) schema in `structured_msg.capnp` is a protocol;
279 * certainly it could change over time: E.g., more types of internal messages might be added.
280 *
281 * This implementation is (we hope) thoughtfully layered, but the question of where exactly lies the separation
282 * between various protocols is a tough one. These aren't just "wire protocols" anymore; there's a programmatic
283 * element to it involving the Struct_builder and Struct_reader concepts. So should there be a separate
284 * negotiation/version for each of these protocols? Which protocols, even? How would this work?
285 *
286 * That's probably the wrong question, we think. Let's instead be pragmatic. Firstly, as of this writing, there *is*
287 * only version V of everything; so it's all moot, until more versions pop up. So all we're trying to do here is
288 * not "shoot ourselves in the foot": Provide some kind of negotiation protocol "base" that all future versions of
289 * the software can count on safely (in the same way we did for the lowest layer). So, really, what we want here
290 * is to have *enough separate protocol versions to negotiate* to be reasonably future-proof, so that future software
291 * won't need component X to be changed even though a protocol in component Y is the one that is changing. So,
292 * pragmatically, speaking:
293 * - We know that just *one* Protocol_negotiator at the struc::sync_io::Channel layer is *sufficient*: In the worst
294 * case the version in it will need to be bumped up without struc::sync_io::Channel code otherwise needing it, but
295 * on account of something outside that class needing a protocol change (e.g., if shm::Builder + shm::Reader encode
296 * SHM stuff differently in the future). So any other `Protocol_negotiator`s we add around here are gravy.
297 * - Exchanging more version numbers (via more `Protocol_negotiator`s) at the same time is nice and efficient and
298 * simple, if indeed we do want the aforementioned "gravy." We just need to identify likely candidates for
299 * future protocol changes. However many such versions we'll decide upon, we can have those Protocol_negotiator
300 * members (at least 1; more for the "gravy") inside `*this`, and we can compactly exchange these in a leading
301 * message sent in either direction. E.g., if there are 3 `Protocol_negotiator`s, we'll send 3 versions
302 * (as of this writing V, V, V) and expect 3 versions to be received similarly. (As usual, on receipt,
303 * each Protocol_negotiator::compute_negotiated_proto_ver() will determine the version to speak -- as of this
304 * writing either V, or *explode the channel due to negotiation failure*.)
305 * - To identify the likely candidates, we should think of it in terms of pieces of software/modules that would
306 * change -- as opposed to the highly subjective notion of which things constitute separate protocols.
307 * This is really not so daunting:
308 * - There is *us*: struc::sync_io::Channel, and the satellite code, especially `structured_msg.capnp`.
309 * This covers a ton of stuff/logic/concepts/terminology; really everything up to but not including the
310 * zero-copy/SHM layer(s) *potentially* also involved.
311 * - It *does* include Heap_fixed_builder and Heap_reader. Sure, they're "merely" impls of the concepts
312 * Struct_builder and Struct_reader, respectively, but those heap-based impls (1) live in our same namespace
313 * ipc::transport::struc and in the same module/library `ipc_transport_structured`; and (2) in practice
314 * are essentially-necessary building blocks for any zero-copy-based `Struct_*er`s including
315 * shm::Builder and shm::Reader. That is to say, there is no point in having some kind of separate version
316 * for struc::sync_io::Channel and co., versus `struc::Heap_*er`.
317 * - There is our sub-namespace, transport::struc::shm -- especially shm::Builder and shm::Reader: this protocol
318 * determines how SHM handles are encoded inside the unstructured blobs transmitted via unstructured `Channel`,
319 * and how they are then interpreted as capnp messages (whether internal or user ones).
320 * - Formally speaking, though, all that is determined at compile time via `Struct_*er_config` template params
321 * to `*this`. As of this writing those are likely to just be either vanilla `"Heap_*er::Config"`, or
322 * shm::Builder::Config + shm::Reader::Config; but formally any Struct_builder / Struct_reader concept impls
323 * are allowed. (The user may well implement their own fanciness.)
324 * - So really it's not about transport::struc::shm specifically but more like, formally speaking,
325 * #Builder_config + #Reader_config protocol code, excluding the base/vanilla
326 * Heap_fixed_builder and Heap_reader (which, we've established, are already covered by the first, non-gravy
327 * Protocol_negotiator).
328 *
329 * Thus it should be sufficient to have:
330 * - Protocol_negotiator for us. That is #m_protocol_negotiator.
331 * - (Possibly unused) Protocol_negotiator for any additional protocol(s) involved in `Struct_*er_config` layer,
332 * such as the existing shm::Builder and shm::Reader. That is #m_protocol_negotiator_aux.
333 * The actual preferred (highest) and lowest-supported Protocol_negotiator::proto_ver_t values shall
334 * as of this writing simply be V; but once that changes we'll likely add some `static constexpr` values
335 * in Struct_builder and Struct_reader concepts (and impls), and `*this` will pass those to Protocol_negotiator
336 * ctor (instead of simply passing Vs).
337 * - (Depending on whether the hypothetical multi-version protocol(s) support backwards-compatibility with
338 * earlier protocol-versions (i.e., a given version range is not [V, V]), we might need more logic/APIs,
339 * so that a given module knows which protocol-version to in fact speak. To reiterate, currently, we need not
340 * worry about it: just don't shoot selves in foot in this version V of everything.)
341 *
342 * Of course even *more* protocols may be involved inside `Struct_*er_config` layer; as of this writing there isn't --
343 * it's just shm::Builder and shm::Reader in practice -- but there can be other `Struct_*er` concept impls which
344 * could be arbitrarily complex. However, we needn't invent some complicated ultra-dynamic/future-proof thing to cover
345 * those possibilities: if it comes down to it, more protocol negotiation can be coded within those protocols themselves
346 * as needed, or one can just bump up the #m_protocol_negotiator_aux version to cover all protocol changes at that
347 * layer.
348 *
349 * That brings us to the mechanics of actually exchanging the highest-protocol-version for each of
350 * #m_protocol_negotiator and #m_protocol_negotiator_aux. We choose to use a very simple and small
351 * capnp-backed (see `struct ProtocolNegotiation` in `structured_msg.capnp`) blob sent before any other out-messages
352 * (and therefore expected before any in-messages). Following the lead of the lower levels:
353 * - Outgoing: ASAP (so start_ops()), `.send_blob/native_handle()` the `ProtocolNegotiation`-storing blob. The
354 * `.send*()`s are all non-blocking and synchronous, so that's simple.
355 * - Incoming: Just before invoking the first receive API (`.async_receive_blob*()`,
356 * `.async_receive_native_handle*()`) -- which occurs in start_and_poll() -- on #m_channel, `.async_receive_blob()`
357 * the `ProtocolNegotiation`-storing blob. Only proceed with the first "real" receive on successful async-receive
358 * of the `ProtocolNegotiation`-storing blob. (Note: all this begins in start_and_poll().)
359 *
360 * There is one slight complication there: underlying #Owned_channel might have 2 pipes (at compile-time), one for
361 * native-handle-bearing messages, one for the converse. The unlikely-but-possible racing of messages being sent
362 * over 2 pipes in ~parallel is normally resolved via message IDs (sequence numbers), but of course we don't want to
363 * include these trivial negotiating leading messages in that mechanism. So: we simply send (and expect)
364 * the negotiation message along *each* pipe, before any others in that pipe. Chronologically speaking, then, the 1st
365 * negotiation-in-message to be received is processed; the other ignored (and trusted to be duplicate of the winner).
366 * There's a bit of negligible overhead, but the important thing is that no "real" messages are processed before
367 * protocol-negotiation phase passes.
368 *
369 * @endinternal
370 *
371 * @tparam Owned_channel_t
372 * See #Async_io_obj doc header.
373 * @tparam Msg_body_t
374 * See #Async_io_obj doc header.
375 * @tparam Builder_config_t
376 * See #Async_io_obj doc header.
377 * @tparam Reader_config_t
378 * See #Async_io_obj doc header.
379 */
380template<typename Owned_channel_t, typename Msg_body_t,
381 typename Builder_config_t, typename Reader_config_t>
382class Channel :
383 public Channel_base,
384 private boost::noncopyable,
385 public flow::log::Log_context
386{
387public:
388 // Types.
389

391 using Async_io_obj = transport::struc::Channel<Owned_channel_t, Msg_body_t,
392 Builder_config_t, Reader_config_t>;
393 /// You may disregard.
394 using Sync_io_obj = Null_peer;
395
396 /// See #Async_io_obj counterpart.
397 using Owned_channel = Owned_channel_t;
398
399 static_assert(Owned_channel::S_IS_SYNC_IO_OBJ,
400 "struc::Channel (whether sync_io or async-I/O) subsumes sync_io-pattern-peer-bearing "
401 "`Channel`s only. Fortunately ipc::session at least emits such `Channel`s.");
402
403 /// See #Async_io_obj counterpart.
404 using Builder_config = Builder_config_t;
405 /// See #Async_io_obj counterpart.
406 using Reader_config = Reader_config_t;
407
408 /// See #Async_io_obj counterpart.
409 using Msg_body = Msg_body_t;
410
411 /// See #Async_io_obj counterpart.
412 using Msg_which = typename Msg_body_t::Which;
413
414 /// See #Async_io_obj counterpart.
415 using Msg_which_in = Msg_which;
416
417 /// See #Async_io_obj counterpart.
418 using Msg_which_out = Msg_which;
419
420 /// See #Async_io_obj counterpart.
421 using Msg_out = struc::Msg_out<Msg_body, typename Builder_config::Builder>;
422
423 /// See #Async_io_obj counterpart.
424 using Msg_in = struc::Msg_in<Msg_body, Reader_config>;
425
426 /// See #Async_io_obj counterpart.
427 using Msg_in_ptr = boost::shared_ptr<Msg_in>;
428
429 /// List of in-messages used in certain APIs like expect_msgs() to synchronously emit cached in-messages.
430 using Msgs_in = std::vector<Msg_in_ptr>;
431
432 /// See #Async_io_obj counterpart.
433 using msg_id_out_t = Channel_base::msg_id_out_t;
434
435 // Constructors/destructor.
436
437 /**
438 * Non-tag, no-log-in ctor form: Creates structured channel peer with no log-in phase (log-in phase must have occurred
439 * in a preceding struc::Channel called *session master channel*), the session token already known and passed-in
440 * to this ctor. Consider also:
441 * - A tag-form ctor (usually simpler than manually cting `struct_builder_config` and
442 * `struct_reader_config`).
443 * - With-log-in ctor (usually needed for session master channel only).
444 *
445 * @note This ctor form is forwarded-to from #Async_io_obj ctor. Documentation below applies to both ctors
446 * except where noted.
447 *
448 * If `*this` ctor is for sync_io::Channel: You'll need to start_ops() (possibly preceded by
449 * replace_event_wait_handles()) per `sync_io` pattern. (If `*this` ctor is for #Async_io_obj: not applicable.)
450 * Then:
451 *
452 * You may send() (et al) immediately after this. However no in-messages shall be emitted, regardless of registered
453 * expectations such as via expect_msg(), until you invoke start_and_poll(). (For #Async_io_obj:
454 * transport::struc::Channel::start().)
455 *
456 * Consider, also, `owned_channel_mutable()->auto_ping()` and/or `owned_channel_mutable()->idle_timer_run()`,
457 * if you desire these features to be ambiently enabled. See Channel::auto_ping(), Channel::idle_timer_run()
458 * for background.
459 *
460 * ### How/whether to obtain a #Builder_config `struct_builder_config` (and related) ###
461 * It is easiest, usually, to use a different ctor form instead; namely use a tagged-ctor version that will
462 * set everything up. See `Channel_base::Serialize_via_*`. Only use the present ctor form:
463 * - IF: your serialization strategy of choice is simply not covered by the tagged-ctor versions available
464 * (you have a custom builder/reader you want to use for advanced purposes). OR:
465 * - IF: you want to use a different serialization strategy in the outgoing direction versus incoming direction:
466 * e.g., this side sends only short things -- and you want to use Heap_fixed_builder here and
467 * Heap_reader there; but the other side sends huge things, so you want SHM-based serialization there
468 * and deserialization here. The tag ctors assume symmetry and don't support this.
469 *
470 * If you've chosen to use this ctor form:
471 *
472 * Formally speaking it's simply up to you to construct these args before calling this ctor; see the docs for
473 * the particular #Builder_config class of choice. Informally: if you're constructing the #Builder_config
474 * and/or specifying `struct_lender_session` (less so #Reader_config, but for consistency it too) directly, you're
475 * probably not doing the right thing. The following places are available to obtain these for safety and
476 * efficiency (and code maintainability):
477 * - From another, compatible, `Channel` via struct_builder_config(), struct_lender_session(),
478 * struct_reader_config().
479 * - Heap-backed:
480 * - `struct_lender_session` is always `NULL_SESSION`. As for the other 2:
481 * - Via `static` heap_fixed_builder_config() and heap_reader_config().
482 * - Via session::Session_mv::heap_reader_config().
483 * - SHM-backed (using SHM-classic as example):
484 * - session::shm::classic::Session_mv::session_shm_builder_config() (ditto reader),
485 * session::shm::classic::Session_mv::session_shm_lender_session(),
486 * session::shm::classic::Session_mv::app_shm_builder_config() (ditto reader),
487 * session::shm::classic::Session_mv::app_shm_lender_session(). Requires a `Session` object.
488 * - session::shm::classic::Session_server::app_shm_builder_config() (requires session::Client_app).
489 * Server-only; if a `Session` is not available or applicable.
490 *
491 * @param logger_ptr
492 * Logger to use for logging subsequently.
493 * @param channel
494 * Channel in PEER state with no prior traffic. All configurations (1 pipe, 2 pipes) are supported.
495 * If `channel.initialized()` is `false`, behavior is undefined (assertion may trip): suggest
496 * sanity-checking this prior to this ctor.
497 * Behavior is undefined if it is not in PEER state or has had prior traffic. (Reminder: PEER state
498 * does not mean it isn't hosed from error/whatever: This is handled gracefully.)
499 * The channel is moved-into `*this`.
500 * @param struct_builder_config
501 * The serialization engine config to use for serializing out-messages. This small object is copied.
502 * @param struct_lender_session
503 * See Struct_builder::Session (and/or Struct_builder::emit_serialization()) concept doc header.
504 * This small value (typically a pointer) is copied; or the type may be Null_session which is empty;
505 * then there is nothing to even copy.
506 * @param struct_reader_config
507 * The deserialization engine config to use for deserializing in-messages. This small object is copied.
508 * @param session_token_non_nil
509 * The session token to place into all out-messages and for which value to check against all in-messages.
510 * If a check fails, the channel is hosed immediately. Behavior undefined if it equals nil
511 * (assertion may trip). See class doc header regarding how to obtain the value to pass-in here.
512 */
513 explicit Channel(flow::log::Logger* logger_ptr, Owned_channel&& channel,
514 const Builder_config& struct_builder_config,
515 const typename Builder_config::Builder::Session& struct_lender_session,
516 const Reader_config& struct_reader_config,
517 const Session_token& session_token_non_nil);
518
519 /**
520 * Non-tag, with-log-in ctor form: Creates structured channel peer (endpoint of the *session master channel*)
521 * with a log-in phase, this peer being the *server* or *client* depending on the arg `is_server`. Consider also:
522 * - A tag-form ctor (usually simpler than manually cting `struct_builder_config` and
523 * `struct_reader_config`).
524 * - No-log-in ctor (since present ctor is usually needed for session master channel only).
525 *
526 * No general user communication can occur until the log-in phase is completed. As such `*this` would be
527 * the *session master channel* with, presumably, exactly 1 such `*this` in the entire process at a given time.
528 * See #Async_io_obj class doc header for background.
529 *
530 * @note This ctor form is forwarded-to from #Async_io_obj ctor. Documentation below applies to both ctors
531 * except where noted.
532 *
533 * If `*this` ctor is for sync_io::Channel: You'll need to start_ops() (possibly preceded by
534 * replace_event_wait_handles()) per `sync_io` pattern. (If `*this` ctor is for #Async_io_obj: not applicable.)
535 * Then:
536 *
537 * You may send() (et al) immediately after this. However no in-messages shall be emitted, regardless of registered
538 * expectations such as via expect_msg(), until you invoke start_and_poll(). (For #Async_io_obj:
539 * transport::struc::Channel::start().)
540 *
541 * Consider, also, `owned_channel_mutable()->auto_ping()` and/or `owned_channel_mutable()->idle_timer_run()`,
542 * if you desire these features to be ambiently enabled. See Channel::auto_ping(), Channel::idle_timer_run()
543 * for background.
544 *
545 * ### As server ###
546 * To begin the log-in phase -- and thus start to move to the logged-in phase, in which general traffic can
547 * occur -- you must use expect_log_in_request(). `*this` will proceed to logged-in phase automatically once
548 * the log-in request message `M` arrives, and you then invoke `send(&X, M)`, where `X` is the log-in response
549 * out-message you create/fill-out. To be clear the phase change occurs as the last step in that
550 * successful send().
551 *
552 * ### As client ###
553 * To begin the log-in phase -- and thus start to move to the logged-in phase, in which general traffic can
554 * occur -- you must `send(&X, nullptr, nullptr, F)`, where `X` is the log-in request out-message you create/fill-out,
555 * while `F()` is the handler for the log-in response. `*this` will proceed to logged-in phase
556 * automatically once the response to X arrives; and will then invoke `F()` for any further validation the
557 * user may desire.
558 *
559 * ### How/whether to obtain a #Builder_config `struct_builder_config` (and #Reader_config similarly) ###
560 * See notes for the other (no-log-in) non-tag ctor overload.
561 *
562 * @param logger_ptr
563 * See other ctor overload.
564 * @param channel
565 * See other ctor overload.
566 * @param struct_builder_config
567 * See other ctor overload.
568 * @param struct_lender_session
569 * See other ctor overload.
570 * @param struct_reader_config
571 * See other ctor overload.
572 * @param is_server
573 * See above.
574 */
575 explicit Channel(flow::log::Logger* logger_ptr, Owned_channel&& channel,
576 const Builder_config& struct_builder_config,
577 const typename Builder_config::Builder::Session& struct_lender_session,
578 const Reader_config& struct_reader_config,
579 bool is_server);
580

802 bool replace_event_wait_handles(const Create_ev_wait_hndl_func& create_ev_wait_hndl_func);

804 /**
805 * Sets up the `sync_io`-pattern interaction between `*this` and the user's event loop; required before
806 * start_and_poll() (and subsequent in-message-related work) and send() (and other out-message-related APIs)
807 * will work (as opposed to no-op/return `false`).
808 *
809 * `ev_wait_func()` -- with signature matching util::sync_io::Event_wait_func -- is a key function memorized
810 * by `*this`. It shall be invoked by `*this` operations when some op cannot complete synchronously and requires
811 * a certain event (readable/writable) to be active on a certain native-handle.
812 *
813 * @see util::sync_io::Event_wait_func doc header for useful and complete instructions on how to write an
814 * `ev_wait_func()` properly. Doing so correctly is the crux of using the `sync_io` pattern.
815 *
816 * This is a standard `sync_io`-pattern API per util::sync_io doc header.
817 *
818 * @tparam Event_wait_func_t
819 * Function type matching util::sync_io::Event_wait_func.
820 * @param ev_wait_func
821 * See above.
822 * @return `false` if this has already been invoked; no-op logging aside. `true` otherwise.
823 */
824 template<typename Event_wait_func_t>
825 bool start_ops(Event_wait_func_t&& ev_wait_func);
826
827 /**
828 * Permanently memorizes the incoming-direction on-error handler, thus authorizing the emission of any
829 * in-messages (and/or an error) to handlers registered via this call, `expect_*()`, async_request(),
830 * `set_*unexpected_response_handler()`; and *synchronously* executes any immediately relevant such handlers
831 * due to pending in-traffic.
832 *
833 * To be clear: the caller must be ready for 0+ (potentially many) handlers to be synchronously invoked by
834 * this call. Even `on_err_func()` itself may be executed. That said, recursive-mayhem is unlikely to be a concern,
835 * since start_and_poll() itself is a one-time operation for a given `*this`.
836 *
837 * Until this is invoked, any incoming lower-level traffic is nevertheless saved in this process's or
838 * opposing process's user RAM to be emitted as required by, and after, start_and_poll(). Therefore there is no
839 * need to worry about in-traffic disappearing without a trace due to start_and_poll() being invoked too late.
840 *
841 * @tparam Task_err
842 * Handler type matching signature of `flow::async::Task_asio_err`.
843 * @param on_err_func
844 * The permanent on-channel-hosed error handler. See class doc header for discussion of error semantics.
845 * @return `true` on success; `false` if start_ops() not yet called, or if already `start_and_poll()`ed, or if a
846 * prior error outgoing-direction error has hosed the owned Channel (then no-op).
847 */
848 template<typename Task_err>
849 bool start_and_poll(Task_err&& on_err_func);

913 /**
914 * Registers the expectation (which may be immediately met) of up to 1 *notification* in-message
915 * whose #Msg_which equals `which`. No-op and return `false` if `which` is already being expected, if log-in phase
916 * is not yet completed, or if a prior error has hosed the owned Channel.
917 *
918 * The expectation is unregistered upon receipt of the applicable in-message (and firing it with that in-message
919 * #Msg_in_ptr as arg). In addition:
920 *
921 * The 1 expected in-message may already be available synchronously. In that case:
922 * - `*qd_msg` shall be loaded with that message; and it is purged from `*this`. You must handle it as you see
923 * fit upon return from this method.
924 * - The expectation is immediately unregistered.
925 * - `on_msg_func` is ignored (it is not memorized).
926 *
927 * Therefore `on_msg_func()` can *only* execute upon a future `sync_io`-pattern async-wait firing its
928 * `(*on_active_ev_func)()`.
929 *
930 * @tparam On_msg_handler
931 * Handler type for in-messages; see class doc header for in-message handling signature.
932 * @param which
933 * Top-level #Msg_body union `which()` value to expect.
934 * @param qd_msg
935 * `*qd_msg` is set to null if no message is immediately available; else set to that message (see above).
936 * @param on_msg_func
937 * `on_msg_func(M)` shall be invoked in the manner explained in class doc header,
938 * on receipt of message with `which() == which`; unless it is immediately available and
939 * therefore loaded into `*qd_msg`.
940 * @return `true` on success; `false` due to one of the above conditions.
941 */
942 template<typename On_msg_handler>
943 bool expect_msg(Msg_which_in which, Msg_in_ptr* qd_msg, On_msg_handler&& on_msg_func);
944
945 /**
946 * In log-in phase as server only: Registers the expectation (which may be immediately met) of up to 1
947 * *log-in request* in-message whose #Msg_which equals `which`. No-op and return `false` if
948 * expect_log_in_request() has already been invoked, if log-in phase is
949 * not active or active in the client role, or if a prior error has hosed the owned Channel.
950 *
951 * The expectation is unregistered upon receipt of the applicable in-message (and firing it with that in-message
952 * #Msg_in_ptr as arg). In addition:
953 *
954 * The 1 expected in-message may already be available synchronously. In that case:
955 * - `*qd_msg` shall be loaded with that message; and it is purged from `*this`. You must handle it as you see
956 * fit upon return from this method.
957 * - The expectation is immediately unregistered.
958 * - `on_log_in_req_func` is ignored (it is not memorized).
959 *
960 * Therefore `on_log_in_req_func()` can *only* execute upon a future `sync_io`-pattern async-wait firing its
961 * `(*on_active_ev_func)()`.
962 *
963 * ### Corner case: mismatched already-received log-in request ###
964 * If the opposing peer's log-in request has already arrived, and its #Msg_which does not equal `which`:
965 * the channel is hosed with error::Code::S_STRUCT_CHANNEL_GOT_UNEXPECTED_LOG_IN_REQUEST, and the on-error
966 * handler (see start_and_poll()) fires *synchronously*, within the present call -- the one exception, besides
967 * start_and_poll() itself, to the rule that only event processing invokes handlers. `true` is returned in
968 * that case (the operation ran and reported its result; `false` is reserved for the no-op conditions above).
969 *
970 * ### Tips ###
971 * Informally the proper behavior is:
972 * -# Construct in log-in-as-server phase.
973 * -# Invoke expect_log_in_request().
974 * -# Await `on_log_in_req_func(X&&)` firing, or immediate delivery of `X` via `*qd_msg`,
975 * where X is the log-in request.
976 * -# After `on_log_in_req_func(X&&)` handler, or immediate delivery of `X` via `*qd_msg`:
977 * check X for correctness (such as process identity checks).
978 * If it fails checks, destroy `*this`; else:
979 * -# Fill out `X = this->create_msg()` (the log-in response) as needed via `X->body_root()`.
980 * -# `send(&X)`. The latter automatically moves `*this` to logged-in phase locally: the bulk of the
981 * API becomes available.
982 *
983 * @tparam On_msg_handler
984 * See expect_msg().
985 * @param which
986 * See expect_msg().
987 * @param qd_msg
988 * See expect_msg().
989 * @param on_log_in_req_func
990 * See above.
991 * @return `true` on success; `false` due to one of the above conditions.
992 */
993 template<typename On_msg_handler>
994 bool expect_log_in_request(Msg_which_in which, Msg_in_ptr* qd_msg, On_msg_handler&& on_log_in_req_func);
995
996 /**
997 * Registers the expectation (some of which may be immediately met) of 0+ *notification* in-messages whose
998 * #Msg_which equals `which`. No-op and return `false` if `which` is already being expected, if log-in phase
999 * is not yet completed, or if a prior error has hosed the owned Channel.
1000 *
1001 * The expectation is unregistered upon subsequent `undo_expect_msgs(which)`.
1002 *
1003 * 1+ expected in-messages may already be available synchronously. In that case:
1004 * - `*qd_msgs` is loaded with those messages; and they are purged from `*this`. You must handle them as you
1005 * see fit upon return from this method.
1006 * - The expectation continues to be registered; `on_msg_func()` may be invoked in the future.
1007 *
1008 * Therefore `on_msg_func()` can *only* execute upon a future `sync_io`-pattern async-wait firing its
1009 * `(*on_active_ev_func)()`.
1010 *
1011 * @tparam On_msg_handler
1012 * See expect_msg().
1013 * @param which
1014 * See expect_msg().
1015 * @param qd_msgs
1016 * `*qd_msgs` is cleared; then filled with any messages (possibly none) immediately available.
1017 * @param on_msg_func
1018 * See above and expect_msg().
1019 * @return See expect_msg().
1020 */
1021 template<typename On_msg_handler>
1022 bool expect_msgs(Msg_which_in which, Msgs_in* qd_msgs, On_msg_handler&& on_msg_func);
1023
