1194 /// The state of `*this` (given start_ops() success); see #m_phase.
1195 enum class Phase
1196 {
1197 /**
1198 * Regular-operation phase: the general API (expect_msg(), etc.) is available. Most `struc::Channel`s
1199 * begin in this phase, via ctor that takes `session_token_non_nil`. This is the terminal phase.
1200 * Phases that lead to it are `S_SRV_LOG_IN` and `S_CLI_LOG_IN`.
1201 */
1202 S_LOGGED_IN,
1203
1204 /**
1205 * Logging-in phase, as server process: The general API (expect_msg(), etc.) is unavailable; only
1206 * expect_log_in_request() and send() are available. This is an initial phase for a *session master channel*,
1207 * via ctor that does not take `session_token_non_nil` and has `is_server == true`. Leads to `S_LOGGED_IN`.
1208 */
1209 S_SRV_LOG_IN,
1210
1211 /**
1212 * Logging-in phase, as client process: The general API (expect_msg(), etc.) is unavailable; only
1213 * create_msg() and send() (response-expecting form) are available. This is an initial phase for
1214 * a *session master channel*, via ctor that does not take `session_token_non_nil` and has `is_server == false`.
1215 * Leads to `S_LOGGED_IN`.
1216 */
1217 S_CLI_LOG_IN
1218 }; // enum class Phase
1219
1220 /**
1221 * Policy for how to act upon receiving an expected message of one kind or another. As of this writing
1222 * there are two applicable scenarios:
1223 * - receiving a response in-message that indicates its originating out-message is
1224 * the message associated with this object in #Expecting_response_map;
1225 * - receiving an in-message whose top-level-union #Msg_which_in `enum` equals the
1226 * #Msg_which_in associated with this object in #Expecting_msg_map.
1227 *
1228 * For the former see Expecting_response as well.
1229 */
1230 struct Expecting_msg
1231 {
1232 // Types.
1233
1234 /// Short-hand to cheap handle type.
1235 using Ptr = boost::movelib::unique_ptr<Expecting_msg>;
1236
1237 // Data.
1238
1239 /**
1240 * `true` if receiving the expected in-message means the expectation is satisfied; `false` if an `undo_*()`
1241 * must be invoked to mark it satisfied. This controls the mechanism by which an Expecting_msg is removed
1242 * from the expected-messages map (#Expecting_response_map, #Expecting_msg_map), freeing
1243 * the non-zero RAM (at least) resource involved.
1244 */
1245 bool m_one_expected;
1246
1247 /**
1248 * The handler to invoke on receiving the expected in-message.
1249 *
1250 * The `shared_ptr` wrapper is because in case of #m_one_expected being `false` we have to copy it when
1251 * `handlers_post()`ing; `move()` could destroy it (leave it `.empty()`) instead.
1252 */
1253 On_msg_handler_ptr m_on_msg_func;
1254 }; // struct Expecting_msg
1255
1256 /**
1257 * Policy for how to act upon receiving a response in-message that indicates its originating out-message is
1258 * the message associated with this object in #Expecting_response_map.
1259 *
1260 * @note Attention: It builds on Expecting_msg.
1261 */
1262 struct Expecting_response : public Expecting_msg
1263 {
1264 // Types.
1265
1266 /// Short-hand to cheap handle type.
1267 using Ptr = boost::movelib::unique_ptr<Expecting_response>;
1268
1269 // Data.
1270
1271 /// Time point when this request was sent; used for one-off RTT histogram in stat::Channel_stats.
1272 util::Fine_time_pt m_sent_when;
1273 }; // struct Expecting_response
1274
1275 /**
1276 * Table mapping originating out-message to the policy for handling an in-message that indicates that out-message
1277 * as the originating message (via message ID -- *after* the out-message is sent via send()).
1278 */
1279 using Expecting_response_map = boost::unordered_flat_map<msg_id_out_t, typename Expecting_response::Ptr>;
1280
1281 /**
1282 * Table mapping in-message #Msg_which_in `enum` value to the policy for handling an in-message with that
1283 * `which()` value.
1284 */
1285 using Expecting_msg_map = boost::unordered_flat_map<Msg_which_in, typename Expecting_msg::Ptr>;
1286
1287 /// Like #Msg_in_ptr but `unique_ptr` instead of `shared_ptr`. Note the latter can upgrade-from a `move()`d former.
1288 using Msg_in_ptr_uniq = boost::movelib::unique_ptr<Msg_in>;
1289
1290 /**
1291 * Short-hand for queue (FIFO) of in-messages.
1292 *
1293 * ### Rationale: Why `queue<boost::container::deque>`? ###
1294 * By default `queue<>` would wrap `std::deque`, but we swap-in a Boost variant `deque`. Reason:
1295 * `std::deque`, in GNU's impl with gcc-9 at least, has move ctor lacking `noexcept`; and it
1296 * allocates when empty. The former matters, as #m_rcv_pending_msgs holds `Msg_in_q`s; and
1297 * as a `_flat_map` relocates its elements on rehash. This "relocates" is by move, only if move is `noexcept`;
1298 * else it is by copy. This would not compile (we have `unique_ptr` elements, and `unique_ptr` is famously
1299 * move-only, non-copyable). `boost::container::deque` has `noexcept` moving, so there is no problem.
1300 */
1301 using Msg_in_q = std::queue<Msg_in_ptr_uniq, boost::container::deque<Msg_in_ptr_uniq>>;
1302
1303 /**
1304 * Reassembly queue type: "queue" of all in-messages with #msg_id_in_t exceeding #m_rcv_msg_next_id, sorted
1305 * in increasing order by that #msg_id_in_t (sequence #). Relevant only if `Owned_channel::S_HAS_2_PIPES == true`.
1306 */
1307 using Reassembly_q = std::map<msg_id_in_t, Msg_in_ptr_uniq>;
1308
1309 /**
1310 * An `enum` with 3 values we use to encode lead-message-has-handle-or-not expectation policy:
1311 * `Tribool_vals::true_value` (lead message must have a native handle), `Tribool_vals::false_value`
1312 * (must have no native handle), `Tribool_vals::indeterminate_value` (either is allowed).
1313 *
1314 * ### Rationale ###
1315 * We do not use an actual `tribool`, because the tricky `==` and `!=` semantics (where it results in a
1316 * `tribool` whose conversion to `bool` has subtle semantics we do not want) invite bugs. We just use
1317 * its `enum` whose meanings fit our desired ones nicely.
1318 */
1319 using Tribool = boost::logic::tribool::value_t;
1320
1321 /// See #Tribool.
1322 using Tribool_vals = boost::logic::tribool;
1323
1324 /**
1325 * Data and policy with respect to receipt of the next/currently-incomplete in-message. Depending on whether
1326 * 1 or 2 in-pipes are enabled in #Owned_channel, and in the former case what kind of in-pipe it is
1327 * (see Channel::S_HAS_BLOB_PIPE, Channel::S_HAS_NATIVE_HANDLE_PIPE, and similar), there
1328 * may be 1 or 2 of these objects (sets of policy + state) in `*this`. See #m_rcv_pipes
1329 * (null pointer being used to permanently disable up to 1 of them) of this type.
1330 *
1331 * As a general rule:
1332 * - Information that never changes about a given Msg_in_pipe is determined at compile-time and available
1333 * via `static constexpr` and alias members. Do not use non-`constexpr` members (not even `const` ones).
1334 * - The rest is (mutable) state and resides in normal data members.
1335 *
1336 * ### Algorithm/background ###
1337 * The #Owned_channel, potentially being a Native_handle_receiver,
1338 * is possibly capable of receiving unstructured messages, each
1339 * message bearing a blob and, optionally, a #Native_handle. Suppose the opposing peer wants to send
1340 * a structured message M, plus #Native_handle S. The latter can just be sent in a single message.
1341 * The former (M) is serialized into 1 or 2+ RAM blobs (a/k/a segments in capnp parlance), depending on its
1342 * size. This shall *always* be 1 if we are SHM-backed.
1343 *
1344 * Then: the whole structured message M + #Native_handle S shall be sent as:
1345 * -# 1 *lead* message containing:
1346 * -# (as header) mandatory metadata (containing notably the message ID);
1347 * -# (after header) 1st capnp-segment serializing M itself;
1348 * -# 0+ further *continuation* messages serializing the rest of M (more capnp-segments as needed 1 seg = 1 msg).
1349 * (Typically 0; always 0 if SHM-backed.)
1350 *
1351 * There are also internal messages -- presumed rare. These are represented by the bullet point 1.1 only:
1352 * there is just the mdt header; nothing else. The algorithm here operates, therefore, under the assumption
1353 * that each structured message = 1 lead message; plus 0+ continuation messages. However in perf analysis
1354 * one should assume 0 continuation messages, as most messages are user messages, and those usually are serializable
1355 * as just 1 capnp-segment.
1356 *
1357 * `m_incomplete_msg` shall store that state across the 1+ async-reads. Once all the segments (and leading mdt
1358 * header) of a given message have been received and loaded into `*m_incomplete_msg`, it is complete and is
1359 * `move()`d to the next layer, eventually hopefully emitted to the user. So then `m_incomplete_msg` is
1360 * assigned a newly-constructed empty message, until the next async-read feeds the mdt/seg 1 into it -- and so on.
1361 *
1362 * Which pipe is used for these 1+ messages, including the 1st one that includes `Native_handle` S?
1363 * - If Channel::S_HAS_BLOB_PIPE_ONLY is `true`, it is a fatal error. No #Native_handle can be transmitted.
1364 * - If Channel::S_HAS_NATIVE_HANDLE_PIPE_ONLY is `true`, then naturally the handles pipe is used
1365 * (Channel::async_receive_native_handle()) -- it's the only pipe available at any rate.
1366 * - If Channel::S_HAS_2_PIPES is `true`, then:
1367 * - The lead message is expected over the handles pipe (Channel::async_receive_native_handle()), as it's the
1368 * only pipe capable of transporting S.
1369 * - (Attn: subtlety!) The continuation messages are *also* expected over that pipe, even though
1370 * the blobs pipe *is* capable of transporting these. Why? Answer: At this stage we're not dealing with
1371 * the structured layer yet (pre-deserialization which isn't yet possible), so there are no sequence numbers.
1372 * It would require absurd contraptions to distinguish a non-handle-bearing continuation message
1373 * with a handle-bearing lead message from a non-handle-bearing lead message;
1374 * to resolve races between the 2 parallel in-pipes; etc. More on this around the to-do below.
1375 *
1376 * Now assume *no* #Native_handle S wants to be sent with M. The serialization logic is all the same -- there's
1377 * just no S transmitted along with the lead message. The transport media are different; as any pipe can
1378 * transmit these unstructured messages, not needing to transmit these strange native handle thingies. So then
1379 * which pipe is used for these messages?
1380 * - If Channel::S_HAS_BLOB_PIPE_ONLY is `true`, then naturally the blobs pipe is used -- being the only one
1381 * available.
1382 * - If Channel::S_HAS_NATIVE_HANDLE_PIPE_ONLY is `true`, then the handles pipe is used -- being the only one
1383 * available (and perfectly capable of transmitting just-blobs).
1384 * - If Channel::S_HAS_2_PIPES is `true`, then: Although either pipe *could* be used, we use the
1385 * blobs pipe; the idea being that the only reason to configure both pipes in a Channel is for performance
1386 * (certainly it doesn't make anything *simpler* after all), and since the handles-pipe alone was deemed
1387 * insufficient, we'll reserve it for handle-bearing structured user messages only.
1388 * - Perf caveat: Isn't it "giving away" perf to (for the sake of simplicity) send messages
1389 * pertaining to sans-handle lead messages along the handles pipe (and not the blobs pipe)?
1390 * Well, yes, possibly a bit -- but only (1) if a message is handle-bearing in the first place; and (2)
1391 * ifs serialization comprises 2+ segments, not 1 (SHM-backed message = always 1 segment in particular).
1392 * That alone likely puts in mostly-negligible territory, as typically messages are 1-segment.
1393 * Still: Here's a to-do:
1394 *
1395 * @todo Look into the algorithm documented in Channel::Msg_in_pipe wherein (with 2 pipes in the channel)
1396 * some low-level messages associated with handle-bearing user structured messages are sent over the (presumably
1397 * somewhat slower) handles pipe despite, themselves, not containing a native handle being transmitted. See text just
1398 * above this to-do in the code.
1399 *
1400 * That describes what happens for each structured message M, paired with #Native_handle S -- or not paired with it.
1401 * So the question is how to make these possibilities work together. Answer:
1402 *
1403 * To get this to work, depending entirely on `Channel::S_HAS_*`, there are 1 or 2 `Msg_in_pipe`s:
1404 * #m_rcv_pipes, each one's type's #S_LEAD_HNDL_EXPECTATION (compile-time constant from t-param!)
1405 * determining (1) which `async_receive_*()` API will be called; and (2) how the async non-error
1406 * result will be handled. (See start_and_poll() where this is kicked off for the first time,
1407 * meaning each of the 2 `Msg_in_pipe`s is cted, specifying #S_LEAD_HNDL_EXPECTATION forever via t-param.)
1408 * - For a given Msg_in_pipe: when no incomplete message is in-progress (such as the start of `*this`):
1409 * create empty structured #Msg_in (assign to `m_incomplete_msg`), do the appropriate
1410 * `m_channel.async_receive_*()`; then when it async-yields result store the first segment blob
1411 * in it (and native handle if any). If no more segments
1412 * are expected for this structured message, done (`*m_incomplete_msg` can be fed to the next layer).
1413 * Repeat this bullet point (create new #Msg_in, async-read, etc.). Otherwise:
1414 * - `m_incomplete_msg` stays (it is still incomplete). `m_channel.async_receive_blob()` (meaning expect
1415 * an unstructured continuation in-message, and if it somehow includes a #Native_handle, then it's a low-level
1416 * `Channel`-hosing error). When it async-yields result, add it to the structured message
1417 * #Msg_in #m_incomplete_msg. Repeat this bullet point until it is completed, at which point
1418 * done -- #m_incomplete_msg can be fed to the next layer; back to the preceding bullet point
1419 * (create new #Msg_in, async-read, etc.).
1420 *
1421 * If `Owned_channel::S_HAS_2_PIPES`, then 2 `async_receive_*()`s are possible simultaneously,
1422 * and there are indeed 2x Msg_in_pipe in `*this`; one for
1423 * just blobs (#S_LEAD_HNDL_EXPECTATION is `false_value`), one for just blob-and-handle combos
1424 * (#S_LEAD_HNDL_EXPECTATION is `true_value`). They can be interleaved.
1425 * Otherwise there's only 1 Msg_in_pipe, namely:
1426 * - If the 1 pipe is blobs-only, `Owned_channel::S_HAS_BLOB_PIPE_ONLY`: it's, obviously, for just
1427 * blobs (#S_LEAD_HNDL_EXPECTATION is `false_value`).
1428 * - If the 1 pipe is blobs-and-handles, `Owned_channel::S_HAS_NATIVE_HANDLE_PIPE_ONLY`: it's for
1429 * both types of messages (#S_LEAD_HNDL_EXPECTATION is `indeterminate_value`).
1430 *
1431 * @note Detour/update: As noted in daddy Channel class doc header, we now typically make use of batch-receiving
1432 * (unless relevant `Msg_in_pipe::S_RCV_BATCH_SIZE == 1`). The above description essentially holds; just
1433 * potentially many messages are received with one call (`.async_receive_*_batch()`) into the #Owned_channel
1434 * layer. For the purposes of the above discussion one can think of this as the equivalent number of
1435 * `.async_receive_{blob|native_handle}()` calls succeeding synchronously one after the other.
1436 * Anyway the algorithm above holds; just the actual async-read calls are expressed somewhat differently
1437 * from the above text.
1438 *
1439 * @tparam LEAD_HNDL_EXPECTATION
1440 * See #S_LEAD_HNDL_EXPECTATION.
1441 */
1442 template<Tribool LEAD_HNDL_EXPECTATION>
1443 struct Msg_in_pipe
1444 {
1445 // Types and constants.
1446
1447 /**
1448 * A #Tribool specifying the requirement on whether the lead (often only) unstructured message of each
1449 * structured in-message must contain or not contain a native handle. Specific meanings are documented
1450 * in #Tribool doc header. (Also it explains why we avoid actual `tribool` logic and just use it as an `enum`.)
1451 *
1452 * This also contains the information as to which of the two potential pipes of #Owned_channel a `*this` pertains
1453 * to: `false_value` <=> blobs-only pipe of #Owned_channel;
1454 * else (`true_value` or `indeterminate_value`) <=> handles-and-blobs pipe of #Owned_channel.
1455 * To wit see #S_BLOBS_ELSE_HNDLS_PIPE.
1456 */
1457 static constexpr Tribool S_LEAD_HNDL_EXPECTATION = LEAD_HNDL_EXPECTATION;
1458
1459 /// If `true`, this pertains to the blobs-only pipe of #Owned_channel; else to its blobs-and-handles pipe.
1460 static constexpr bool S_BLOBS_ELSE_HNDLS_PIPE = S_LEAD_HNDL_EXPECTATION == Tribool_vals::false_value;
1461
1462 /// Batch-size to use for this pipe (`Channel` carries the concept constant under per-pipe bifurcated names).
1463 static constexpr size_t S_RCV_BATCH_SIZE = S_BLOBS_ELSE_HNDLS_PIPE
1464 ? Owned_channel::S_RCV_BLOB_BATCH_SZ_RECOMMENDATION
1465 : Owned_channel::S_RCV_NATIVE_HANDLE_BATCH_SZ_RECOMMENDATION;
1466 static_assert(S_RCV_BATCH_SIZE >= 1,
1467 "Batch must be able to hold at least one message. `1` would bypass most batching code but work.");
1468
1469 /**
1470 * The type of #m_target_batch: the target (blob(s), handle(s)) of the next unstructured-message async-read.
1471 *
1472 * Note that, as explained in daddy class Channel doc header, we use a simplified code-path if configured
1473 * to use "batches" that are sized 1; that is to not use batch-receiving. So in that case
1474 * the actual #Batch type is Generic_msg_batch_in (which we always set to contain 1 slot at run-time),
1475 * and the async-receiving layer of `Channel` shall simply target slot 0's contained target blob (and possibly
1476 * `Native_handle`), and we don't even let its `.n_used()` change away from 0. Basically it's just a
1477 * buffer/handle store, nothing more.
1478 *
1479 * ### Rationale ###
1480 * In that case why not just store a separate field pair in Msg_in_pipe, like `Segment_blob_in m_target_blob` +
1481 * `Native_handle m_target_hndl`? Answer: Sure, that would've been fine too; then one would just not touch
1482 * `m_target_batch` (it is already `optional` even, for other reason(s)). Doing it this way just seemed like a nice
1483 * compact way (both memory-wise and code-wise) to store it; that's all. Either way is fine. (To be clear
1484 * Generic_msg_batch_in is useful for other purposes; it doesn't just exist for this degenerate use.)
1485 */
1486 using Batch = std::conditional_t<S_RCV_BATCH_SIZE == 1,
1487 Generic_msg_batch_in<Segment_blob_in, S_BLOBS_ELSE_HNDLS_PIPE>,
1488 std::conditional_t
1489 <S_BLOBS_ELSE_HNDLS_PIPE,
1490 typename Owned_channel::template Blob_batch_in<Segment_blob_in>,
1491 typename Owned_channel::template Native_handle_batch_in<Segment_blob_in>>>;
1492 // Data.
1493
1494 /**
1495 * As we are building the current structured #m_incomplete_msg, whether the next unstructured in-message be the
1496 * lead/first (often only) one composing it (`true`); or one of the next ones a/k/a a continuation
1497 * message (`false`). So it starts `false` whenever #m_incomplete_msg is cted; changed to `true` after the lead
1498 * message (if there are continuation messages forthcoming; otherwise #m_incomplete_msg is cted right then again).
1499 *
1500 * @note We could also, conceptually, get this state from #m_incomplete_msg itself. As of this writing there's
1501 * no accessor to the effect of "how many segments ya got?" or "have ya got at least one segment already?"
1502 * in Msg_in_impl or Msg_in, and this flag here seemed like a simple way to keep track of it ourselves.
1503 */
1504 bool m_next_msg_lead_else_cont;
1505
1506 /**
1507 * 0 when #m_next_msg_lead_else_cont is `true`; otherwise: The number of user-message-composing capnp-segments
1508 * still needed **including** the last message (segment) to have been received. Hence once it reaches 1,
1509 * #m_incomplete_msg is complete and must be `move()`d away and cted anew. So it goes like this:
1510 * -# #m_incomplete_msg is cted; #m_next_msg_lead_else_cont set to `true`; we're set to 0.
1511 * -# Read lead msg. Scan the mdt header therein; its Msg_in_impl::deserialize_mdt() returns the initial
1512 * value assigned to us. If we're 0, it's an internal message. If we're 1, it's a user message comprising
1513 * 1 segment (this is good and typical but not universal). Either way #m_incomplete_msg is immediately
1514 * complete: go back to step 1. Otherwise it is 2 or higher.
1515 * -# Read continuation msg. Decrement us. If we're now 1, #m_incomplete_msg is complete: go back to step 1.
1516 * Otherwise it is still 2 or higher. Repeat the present step.
1517 */
1518 size_t m_n_segs_left_pre_last_read;
1519
1520 /**
1521 * See #Batch doc header.
1522 *
1523 * ### Rationale ###
1524 * This type is template-parameterized, so we use method templates of daddy `Channel` to operate on a `*this`;
1525 * and use auto-typed lambda captures of `this` when async-ops are involved. See, relatedly, #m_rcv_pipes doc
1526 * header.
1527 *
1528 * It is `optional` as of this writing only because it is somewhat painful to direct-initialize a `*this`
1529 * otherwise. For all intents and purposes this thing is never null except at the very start.
1530 */
1531 std::optional<Batch> m_target_batch;
1532
1533 /**
1534 * Target (incomplete) in-message for the `async_receive_*()` operation in-progress; one is always in-progress
1535 * once `start_and_poll()` has been called, until the pipe is hosed. Its lifecycle is described in
1536 * #m_n_segs_left_pre_last_read doc header. Some added details as pertains to that:
1537 * - Msg_in_impl::add_serialization_segment() is called to `move()` a #Segment_blob_in (blob) stored inside
1538 * #m_target_batch into this `m_incomplete_msg`. (That slot's blob is then re-allocated for the next time.)
1539 * - The blob's `.capacity()` is unchanged; while `.size()` is adjusted via `.resize()` to reflect the
1540 * actual # of bytes received which may be `<= .capacity()`. We do this just before
1541 * `m_incomplete_msg.add_serialization_segment()`.
1542 * - Msg_in_impl::deserialize_mdt(), called upon receiving the lead message and doing the preceding step,
1543 * returns the # of segments (at least 1).
1544 * - Msg_in_impl::deserialize_body() is called once all segments have been added into this guy.
1545 * As a result Msg_in::body_root() now provides access to the structured (capnp) accessor tree. Done!
1546 * Can emit to user, or at least save at the next layer of daddy `*this` to emit later.
1547 *
1548 * Subtlety: It's a `unique_ptr` (not #Msg_in_ptr `shared_ptr`) for anti-leak safety/perf.
1549 * It is moved and upgraded to a `shared_ptr` (#Msg_in_ptr) when message completed.
1550 */
1551 Msg_in_ptr_uniq m_incomplete_msg;
1552
1553 /**
1554 * Used only for the first/second in-messages in the pipe, before any #m_incomplete_msg, when doing protocol
1555 * negotiation + channel-header grabbing:
1556 * this is the (small) target buffer to the simple `ProtocolNegotiation` capnp-`struct`; then again
1557 * the `ChannelHeader` capnp-`struct`. It is emptied once this procedure finishes (i.e., once #m_incomplete_msg
1558 * is targeted with an async-read for the 1st time).
1559 *
1560 * @note `rcv_past_init_msgs()` relies on the above-implied invariant wherein
1561 * init-msgs procedure ongoing <=> `!m_init_msg_blob.zero()`. Or the inverted version:
1562 * `rcv_async_read()` (main/user-msgs) read-chain started <=> `m_init_msg_blob.zero()`.
1563 */
1564 Segment_blob_in m_init_msg_blob;
1565
1566 /**
1567 * Accompanying #m_init_msg_blob, this is the target `Native_handle` for those initial async-receives (if the
1568 * pipe supports such, else untouched). However: such initial messages shall never include any
1569 * non-null `Native_handle`; but we still need a place to put it for the `.async_receive_native_handle()` API.
1570 *
1571 * @note To maintainers: We plop the non-auto-closing `Native_handle m_init_msg_hndl`'s contents, if any,
1572 * into an auto-closing util::Own_native_handle, so that it does not leak in any scenario. Resist the
1573 * temptation to change that, i.e., to keep the naked `Native_handle` around any longer than absolutely
1574 * necessary.
1575 */
1576 Native_handle m_init_msg_hndl;
1577
1578 /**
1579 * Starts `false`; becomes `true` on detecting error::Code::S_RECEIVES_FINISHED_CANNOT_RECEIVE a/k/a
1580 * graceful-close on a receive op along this pipe. Carries algorithmic meaning if and only if:
1581 * - compile-time Channel::S_HAS_2_PIPES is `true`; *and*
1582 * - `*this Channel` is not yet hosed (#m_channel_err_code_or_ok falsy).
1583 *
1584 * How it is set is very straightforward: as noted, just make it `false` => `true` on detecting
1585 * graceful-close. However, how it is algorithmically used is a different story:
1586 *
1587 * ### Rationale/design ###
1588 * Preamble:
1589 * - Again: If there is only 1 Msg_in_pipe in `*this Channel`, then this is not used; no need to read further.
1590 * - `*this` in the following text refers the sync_io::Channel, not the Msg_in_pipe `struct`.
1591 *
1592 * Consider 1 unstructured-transport pipe that is last-known healthy, while the other pipe is as well; suppose
1593 * a pipe-1 receive (or send for that matter) emits a pipe-hosing error (at the unstructured layer). Should
1594 * this hose `*this` <=> should we set #m_channel_err_code_or_ok to that error? Answer: For almost all errors
1595 * the answer is yes; we made the decision elsewhere that generally if 1 pipe is hosed, we treat the other
1596 * as hosed too. (Why? Primarily it is to keep things as simple as possible; but the defensibility of it is
1597 * as follows: If pipe 1 went down, at least in a machine-local scenario, then overall the channel is no
1598 * longer operating normally; pipe 2 will go down anyway, and there is no point in supporting the no-man's-land
1599 * until this is detected: just hose the whole thing and be done with it.)
1600 *
1601 * There is however exactly one type of pipe 1-hosing error that is the exception to this:
1602 * RECEIVES_FINISHED_CANNOT_RECEIVE a/k/a graceful-close <=> opposing user called async_end_sending() (which
1603 * we do not require but recommend to ensure all messages are delivered; see that guy's doc header for rationale).
1604 * Unlike the other errors, it is not correct to treat this as evidence that both pipes are "really" down.
1605 * It is a normal occurrence; I might send message X, then graceful-close down pipe 2 + graceful-close down
1606 * pipe 1 right in a row; if the pipe-1 graceful-close happens to be detected first, then message X will never
1607 * be delivered to the `*this` user, even if they had a handler waiting for it. The hosing of `*this` would
1608 * cause us to ignore X (e.g., at least via handle_async_err_code() check for already-hosed condition).
1609 *
1610 * Therefore:
1611 * - (As already stipulated: Upon receiving RECEIVES_FINISHED_CANNOT_RECEIVE for either pipe, mark that
1612 * fact by setting its `m_gracefully_closed = true`.)
1613 * - Detecting any pipe-hosing error, including RECEIVES_FINISHED_CANNOT_RECEIVE, *should* end the read
1614 * chain for that pipe. After all, the individual pipe really is hosed: nothing else will arrive by
1615 * definition.
1616 * - Detecting any pipe-hosing error *except* RECEIVES_FINISHED_CANNOT_RECEIVE *should* immediately hose `*this`
1617 * (make #m_channel_err_code_or_ok truthy).
1618 * - However: Detecting RECEIVES_FINISHED_CANNOT_RECEIVE (<=> our own `m_gracefully_closed == true`)
1619 * may or may not hose `*this`. So assuming `*this` is not already hosed anyway:
1620 * -# Check `m_gracefully_closed` **for the other pipe**.
1621 * -# If `false`: Do not hose `*this`. (We're gracefully-hosed; they aren't hosed at all; `*this` can
1622 * still receive in-msgs.)
1623 * -# If `true`: Hose `*this`. (Both pipes have gracefully ended in-traffic. So it is correct to consider
1624 * the overall pipe as "really" down.)
1625 * - ("But is it really-really down? Can't they still send out-traffic potentially?"
1626 * Answer: This it out of scope here. For your convenience though: To keep things simple we don't make
1627 * use of this full-duplex capability of the lower/unstructured layer; if in-pipes are down, we consider
1628 * the out-pipes unusable too <=> `*this` hosed.)
1629 *
1630 * To summarize: Before assigning in-direction error E to #m_channel_err_code_or_ok (thus hosing `*this`),
1631 * where E=graceful-close, first check whether #m_gracefully_closed (on the other pipe!) indicates that
1632 * the *other* pipe also got E earlier; if yes then hose; if not then don't. In the latter case the
1633 * same check would occur for that other pipe on its subsequent detection -- if any -- of E, that time actually
1634 * hosing `*this` upon seeing our `m_gracefully_closed == true`.
1635 *
1636 * ### Patterns (to maintainers) ###
1637 * More text here; some is arguably redundant versus the above; but the goal here is to show the patterns
1638 * w/r/t where this state is relevant/irrelevant, as it could otherwise be daunting to know which exact kind of
1639 * hosedness is relevant in which context.
1640 *
1641 * Setting this flag to `true`: It should be written if, and only if, immediately upon eventful sync or async
1642 * read (<=> got `Error_code` result of `.async_receive_*()` other than would-block) the `Error_code` is in fact
1643 * transport::error::Code::S_RECEIVES_FINISHED_CANNOT_RECEIVE. As of this writing that occurs in a single
1644 * place: handle_async_err_code().
1645 *
1646 * Checking this flag's value, for main algorithmic purposes (as opposed to logging or stats or such), shall
1647 * occur only for the following specific purposes/according to the following patterns.
1648 * -# Upon setting this pipe's flag to `true` (see just above), decide whether to hose `*this`:
1649 * If not already hosed, and there are two pipes, and the other pipe's flag
1650 * (via deref of #m_other_pipe_gracefully_closed_or_null) is already true: hose; else don't.
1651 * - Where: Wherever a pipe's `m_gracefully_closed = true` assignment happens (see just above).
1652 * -# When checking whether to continue this pipe's read chain (basically <=> perform next `async_receive_*()`),
1653 * and this info was not returned helpfully by handle_async_err_code(),
1654 * meaning the question must be answered by looking at `*this` state. So the question boils down to:
1655 * Did *this pipe* (not necessarily all of `*this`) just go from non-hosed to hosed? The pre-state (this
1656 * pipe not hosed) is routinely ascertained throughout the pipe's state machine; so the question reduces
1657 * further to: is *this pipe* (not necessarily all of `*this`) hosed. If there is one pipe then
1658 * that's simply yes <=> `bool(m_channel_err_code_or_ok)`. If there are 2 then: if `*this` is hosed
1659 * (again `bool(m_channel_err_code_or_ok)`), then by definition this pipe is hosed, as both are hosed;
1660 * otherwise if `m_gracefully_closed` then this pipe is hosed. So, given 2 pipes exist: `pipe` hosed <=>
1661 * `m_channel_err_code_or_ok || pipe->m_gracefully_closed`.
1662 * - Where: rcv_end_reads() computes this. Call this; don't directly query `m_gracefully_closed` for
1663 * this algorithmic purpose.
1664 * - But: For perf + cleanliness we'd rather not call rcv_end_reads() -- but merely check
1665 * full-hosedness (`bool(m_channel_err_code_or_ok)`) -- unless necessary. To that end
1666 * consider that `m_gracefully_closed` can only become `true` versus its
1667 * having been `false` in the aforementioned "pre-state" due to handle_async_err_code() (see above).
1668 * More to the point, though, that guy would only possibly detect RECEIVES_FINISHED_CANNOT_RECEIVE
1669 * immediately after pipe's `async_receive_*()`, which is the only relevant operation in the sense that
1670 * it operates at the lower (unstructured-transport, #Owned_channel) layer. The many places where
1671 * we handle_new_error() (=> hose()) with a `struc::`-layer error (protocol misuse usually) cannot
1672 * possibly yield a truthening of `m_gracefully_closed`. Hence this pattern:
1673 * - By default (lots of places): Just check overall-hosedness (`bool(m_channel_err_code_or_ok)`).
1674 * - Except (few places): Immediately following an operation that reacted to an `async_receive_*()` of
1675 * the pipe (<=> internally called handle_async_err_code()): Use rcv_end_reads().
1676 *
1677 * Recap: Set it in one place: handle_async_err_code(). Use it for should-we-hose-`*this` decision in one
1678 * place: handle_async_err_code(). Use it for is-this-pipe-hosed-so-stop-this-read-chain question, if
1679 * handle_async_err_code() did not already return this info, by calling rcv_end_reads(). It is only necessary
1680 * to do that (as opposed to merely `bool(m_channel_err_code_or_ok)`) after an `async_receive_*()` handler
1681 * `rcv_on_async_read_*()`.
1682 */
1683 bool m_gracefully_closed;
1684
1685 /**
1686 * Point to the other `Msg_in_pipe`'s #m_gracefully_closed; or null if `*this Channel` has 1 pipe
1687 * (`Owned_channel::S_HAS_2_PIPES == false`).
1688 *
1689 * ### Rationale ###
1690 * See doc header for #m_gracefully_closed. This is an easy way to check the other's pipe flag's value
1691 * without having to pass both `Msg_in_pipe` objects around all over the place, for this one check.
1692 * (Channel::m_rcv_pipes is available at all times, yes, but its elements are type-erased: the type info
1693 * is a template argument to the various `rcv_...()` methods, but we'd rather not have to include the
1694 * 2nd pipe's type info in the template parameterization.)
1695 */
1696 bool* m_other_pipe_gracefully_closed_or_null;
1697 }; // struct Msg_in_pipe
1698
1699 /**
1700 * Just groups the varieties of user-facing handler executed via handlers_post(); one nested `struct`
1701 * (aggregate) per variety, its `execute()` being what runs.
1702 *
1703 * @see handlers_post() doc header for the handler-posting rules.
1704 *
1705 * To coders/maintainers: a variety object is constructed on the stack and executed immediately; simply keep
1706 * its data members cheap to move-construct (smart pointers, scalars, `string`s...) -- all current ones are.
1707 *
1708 * ### Rationale ###
1709 * Why bother with this, when really every use of `Handlers` resolves to synchronously this:
1710 * stack-construct => `execute()` => stack-destroy; and that itself resolves to "call a particular handler,
1711 * passing it some args," a/k/a calling a `Function`? There would be less boiler-plate if we simply called a
1712 * function.
1713 *
1714 * Answer: It is an intentional ploy to draw attention to the sensitive nature of invoking a user-handler,
1715 * which we call *handler-posting*. This way we explicitly enumerate the varieties of user-handler. So we
1716 * add some boiler-plate but hopefully encourage discipline/deliberateness from maintainers, when it comes
1717 * to handler-posing in `*this` trickier-than-normal state machine.
1718 */
1719 struct Handlers
1720 {
1721 // Types.
1722
1723 /**
1724 * Executor for handler indicating receipt of a message (an expected response as via `async_request()`,
1725 * an expected notification as via `expect_*()`, or an unexpected response as via
1726 * set_unexpected_response_handler()). This is by far the most popular expected variety in Handlers.
1727 */
1728 struct Message
1729 {
1730 // Data.
1731
1732 /// Message that arrived.
1733 Msg_in_ptr_uniq m_msg_in;
1734
1735 /// Handler to execute; or null if the message was an unexpected response.
1736 On_msg_handler_ptr m_on_msg_func_if_expected;
1737
1738 // Methods.
1739
1740 /**
1741 * Executes handler.
1742 * @param daddy
1743 * The containing object.
1744 */
1745 void execute(Channel* daddy);
1746 }; // struct Message
1747
1748 /**
1749 * Executor for handler indicating being informed by opposing side that *it* received a response to a message
1750 * that was not issued as a response-expecting request (as via set_remote_unexpected_response_handler()).
1751 */
1752 struct Remote_unexpected_response
1753 {
1754 // Data.
1755
1756 /**
1757 * As indicated by opposing side, the ID of the message that allegedly requested a response (but
1758 * didn't in fact) according to the metadata of the incoming (to the opposing side) problematic in-message.
1759 */
1760 msg_id_t m_originating_msg_id;
1761
1762 /**
1763 * Explanatory text indicated by the opposing side ostensibly describing various things about
1764 * the problematic in-message (for logging/reporting).
1765 */
1766 std::string m_mdt_text;
1767
1768 // Methods.
1769
1770 /**
1771 * Executes handler.
1772 * @param daddy
1773 * The containing object.
1774 */
1775 void execute(Channel* daddy);
1776 }; // struct Remote_unexpected_response
1777
1778 /// Executor for handler indicating `Channel` error (as via start_and_poll() arg). Empty (`daddy` arg is enough).
1779 struct Error
1780 {
1781 // Methods.
1782
1783 /**
1784 * Executes handler.
1785 * @param daddy
1786 * The containing object.
1787 */
1788 void execute(Channel* daddy);
1789 }; // struct Error
1790 }; // struct Handlers
1791
1792 // Constants.
1793
1794 /// The version of the protocol we speak (see "Protocol negotiation" in class doc header).
1795 static constexpr Protocol_negotiator::proto_ver_t S_PROTOCOL_VERSION_MIN = 2;
1796 /// See #S_PROTOCOL_VERSION_MIN.
1797 static constexpr Protocol_negotiator::proto_ver_t S_PROTOCOL_VERSION_MAX = S_PROTOCOL_VERSION_MIN;
1798
1799 // Methods.
1800
1801 // start_and_poll() pipe: Protocol negotiation/header phase.
1802
1803 /**
1804 * Acts on the pre-condition that the given in-pipe has just started (thus not known to be in would-block state);
1805 * and therefore we should read (and process) as many unstructured in-messages as synchronously possible
1806 * -- starting with the protocol-negotiation in-message -- until reaching would-block state, at which point we
1807 * should `return` with a pending async-wait/read on that in-pipe. Either synchronously or asynchronously
1808 * (across an async-wait) this will ultimately invoke rcv_on_async_read_proto_neg_msg() which, in the best case
1809 * scenario, will move on to the next step: `rcv_async_read_channel_header(pipe)`.
1810 *
1811 * This shall be called in exactly the following situation: start_and_poll().
1812 *
1813 * @param pipe
1814 * Pointer into #m_rcv_pipes array.
1815 */
1816 template<typename Msg_in_pipe_t>
1817 void rcv_async_read_proto_neg_msg(Msg_in_pipe_t* pipe);
1818
1819 /**
1820 * To execute upon completing an `m_channel.async_receive_*()` of the expected protocol-negotiation message along
1821 * the given in-pipe, this processes the result (message or error) and continues the read chain (on negotiation
1822 * success) or ends it (on any failure -- then the on-error handler fires from within; see handlers_post()).
1823 *
1824 * If continuing the read chain: the next link is rcv_async_read_channel_header().
1825 *
1826 * @param pipe
1827 * See rcv_async_read_proto_neg_msg().
1828 * `pipe->m_init_msg_blob` and `pipe->m_init_msg_hndl` may have been received-into.
1829 * @param err_code
1830 * From `Channel::async_receive_*()`.
1831 * @param sz
1832 * From `Channel::async_receive_*()`.
1833 */
1834 template<typename Msg_in_pipe_t>
1835 void rcv_on_async_read_proto_neg_msg(Msg_in_pipe_t* pipe, Error_code err_code, size_t sz);
1836
1837 /**
1838 * Next in the read chain following rcv_on_async_read_proto_neg_msg(), this is similar to
1839 * rcv_async_read_proto_neg_msg() but on success invokes rcv_on_async_read_channel_header() which
1840 * processes the `ChannelHeader` message as opposed to protocol-negotiation message (the preceding thing).
1841 *
1842 * This shall be called in exactly the following situation: rcv_on_async_read_proto_neg_msg().
1843 *
1844 * @param pipe
1845 * Pointer into #m_rcv_pipes array.
1846 */
1847 template<typename Msg_in_pipe_t>
1848 void rcv_async_read_channel_header(Msg_in_pipe_t* pipe);
1849
1850 /**
1851 * This is to rcv_async_read_channel_header() what rcv_on_async_read_proto_neg_msg() is to
1852 * rcv_async_read_proto_neg_msg():
1853 *
1854 * Processes the result (message or error) and continues the read chain (if no error) or ends it (on error --
1855 * then the on-error handler fires from within; see handlers_post()). Processing the result successfully means
1856 * at least saving the relevant `ChannelHeader` info; as of this writing #m_peer_process_creds.
1857 *
1858 * If continuing the read chain: the next link is rcv_async_read().
1859 *
1860 * @param pipe
1861 * See rcv_async_read_channel_header().
1862 * `pipe->m_init_msg_blob` and `pipe->m_init_msg_hndl` may have been received-into.
1863 * @param err_code
1864 * From `Channel::async_receive_*()`.
1865 * @param sz
1866 * From `Channel::async_receive_*()`.
1867 */
1868 template<typename Msg_in_pipe_t>
1869 void rcv_on_async_read_channel_header(Msg_in_pipe_t* pipe, Error_code err_code, size_t sz);
1870
1871 // start_and_poll() pipe: Main phase, unstructured-message layer.
1872
1873 /**
1874 * Assuming `pipe` is live (async-read chain going): returns whether the init-messages phase (protocol negotiation,
1875 * `ChannelHeader`) has passed <=> rcv_async_read() has been called.
1876 *
1877 * @param pipe
1878 * Ref into #m_rcv_pipes array.
1879 * @return `true` if rcv_async_read() has been called; else `false`.
1880 */
1881 template<typename Msg_in_pipe_t>
1882 bool rcv_past_init_msgs(const Msg_in_pipe_t& pipe) const;
1883
1884 /**
1885 * On rcv_on_async_read_channel_header() having received the pipe-leading protocol-negotiation bytes and
1886 * passed #m_protocol_negotiator negotiation and obtained `ChannelHeader`-stored info, this continues the
1887 * read chain by starting the bulk of it, wherein synchronously or asynchronously we are always reading
1888 * the next unstructured in-message -- until error or `*this` destruction.
1889 *
1890 * Compile-time-depending on certain compile-time config, we equal either rcv_async_read_batched() or
1891 * rcv_async_read_unbatched(). The two code paths are mutually exclusive (have conceptual similarities but
1892 * as of this writing ~no common code in `*this` itself) but share the same code at the layer wherein
1893 * a given unstructured in-message (in blob form) is ready for interpretation (complete
1894 * Msg_in_pipe::m_incomplete_msg, send it to user-facing layer... and so on).
1895 *
1896 * @param pipe
1897 * Pointer into #m_rcv_pipes array.
1898 */
1899 template<typename Msg_in_pipe_t>
1900 void rcv_async_read(Msg_in_pipe_t* pipe);
1901
1902 /**
1903 * To be invoked either *as* rcv_async_read() (if we are compile-time-configured to receive unstructured in-messages
1904 * in *batches*) or later in the read-chain upon having obtained (and processed) an
1905 * in-batch (1+ unstructured in-messages).
1906 *
1907 * @param pipe
1908 * Pointer into #m_rcv_pipes array.
1909 * @param pessimistic
1910 * A/k/a `assume_would_block` elsewhere, this shall be `true` if the just-received-and-processed
1911 * in-batch implied would-block -- got 1+ in-messages but fewer than its capacity; or `false` if
1912 * it did not imply it -- got a totally-full in-batch (could mean there's even more to read; could
1913 * mean that's exactly how many were pending, a coincidence).
1914 */
1915 template<typename Msg_in_pipe_t>
1916 void rcv_async_read_batched(Msg_in_pipe_t* pipe, bool pessimistic = false);
1917
1918 /**
1919 * To be invoked either *as* rcv_async_read() (if we are compile-time-configured to not receive unstructured
1920 * in-messages in *batches* but rather one async-read at a time) or later in the read-chain upon having obtained
1921 * (and processed) an unstructured in-message.
1922 *
1923 * @note In particular, it should reduce to *exactly* the same logic as rcv_async_read_batched() if
1924 * the batch-capacity (Msg_in_pipe::S_RCV_BATCH_SIZE) were `1`. Incidentally it lacks `bool pessimistic`,
1925 * because when the capacity is 1, receiving an in-batch (1+ in-messages... so 1 in-message) makes it unclear
1926 * whether the pipe is now in would-block or not; hence `pessimistic = false` always.
1927 *
1928 * @param pipe
1929 * Pointer into #m_rcv_pipes array.
1930 */
1931 template<typename Msg_in_pipe_t>
1932 void rcv_async_read_unbatched(Msg_in_pipe_t* pipe);
1933
1934 /**
1935 * The part of rcv_async_read_batched() algorithm that is "between" any possible async-waits; in other words
1936 * processes an in-batch or an error (but not would-block!) in trying to read such -- but stops before
1937 * perpetuating the read chain even in the former (no-error) case.
1938 *
1939 * If and only #m_channel_err_code_or_ok is truthy on return, stop read chain; else continue it.
1940 *
1941 * @param pipe
1942 * Pointer into #m_rcv_pipes array.
1943 * `*pipe->m_target_batch` contains the updated Msg_batch_in (including Msg_batch_in::n_used() `>= 1`
1944 * indicating how many in-messages were obtained) unless `err_code` truthy.
1945 * @param err_code
1946 * Result of batch read; either falsy (success) or truthy (error but *not* would-block).
1947 * @return If `m_channel_err_code_or_ok` is truthy on return, return `false`, but basically the return value
1948 * should be ignored (channel-hosing error should be checked-for first). Otherwise:
1949 * `true` means no implied would-block; please do another *synchronous* read.
1950 * `false` (with `!m_channel_err_code_or_ok`) means implied would-block;
1951 * do a definitely-asynchronous (for perf) read (since pipe is in would-block).
1952 */
1953 template<typename Msg_in_pipe_t>
1954 bool rcv_on_async_read_batch(Msg_in_pipe_t* pipe, const Error_code& err_code);
1955
1956 /**
1957 * The part of rcv_async_read_unbatched() algorithm that is "between" any possible async-waits; in other words
1958 * processes an in-message or an error (but not would-block!) in trying to read such -- but stops before
1959 * perpetuating the read chain even in the former (no-error) case.
1960 *
1961 * If and only #m_channel_err_code_or_ok is truthy on return, stop read chain; else continue it.
1962 *
1963 * @note In particular, it should reduce to *exactly* the same logic as rcv_on_async_read_batch() if
1964 * the batch-capacity (Msg_in_pipe::S_RCV_BATCH_SIZE) were `1`, and `batch->n_used() == 1`, and
1965 * slot 0's result-payload blob size equaled `sz`. Incidentally it takes `sz`, because
1966 * we do not use Msg_in_pipe::m_target_batch as anything more but a place to store bytes + handle, in its
1967 * slot 0. `.n_used()` would go from 0 to 1 by definition of single-message receive (so no info needed);
1968 * and bytes-received is given to us explicitly by Blob_receiver::async_receive_blob() or
1969 * Native_handle_receiver::async_receive_native_handle() (as `sz`) as opposed to modifying that part of
1970 * slot 0, so we can just pass that to this method. Lastly we return `void`, unlike
1971 * rcv_on_async_read_batch(), as with a 1-batch that guy would always return `true` anyway.
1972 *
1973 * @param pipe
1974 * Pointer into #m_rcv_pipes array.
1975 * `*pipe->m_target_batch` (capacity 1!) slot 0 contains the new in-message unless `err_code` truthy.
1976 * @param err_code
1977 * Result of single-message read; either falsy (success) or truthy (error but *not* would-block).
1978 * @param sz
1979 * If `err_code` falsy, this value (which must be positive) is how many bytes were obtained.
1980 */
1981 template<typename Msg_in_pipe_t>
1982 void rcv_on_async_read_one(Msg_in_pipe_t* pipe, const Error_code& err_code, size_t sz);
1983
1984 /**
1985 * When `pipe->m_next_msg_lead_else_cont == true`:
1986 * Where the rcv_async_read_batched() and rcv_async_read_unbatched() mutually-exclusive code-paths merge again,
1987 * this is where we bridge to the structured-message layer, updating everything in Msg_in_pipe
1988 * except Msg_in_pipe::m_target_batch (the preceding layer/the caller's responsibility still).
1989 *
1990 * More specifically, then: updates `pipe->m_incomplete_msg` with the new unstructured in-message; and
1991 * if that completes the structured in-message, feeds it to the next layer: rcv_struct_new_msg_in().
1992 *
1993 * If and only #m_channel_err_code_or_ok is truthy on return, stop read chain; else continue it.
1994 * The former would occur if `pipe->m_incomplete_msg` is completed by the processed in-message, but
1995 * it is broken somehow (other side didn't follow protocol/bug).
1996 *
1997 * @param pipe
1998 * Pointer into #m_rcv_pipes array.
1999 * @param target_blob_ptr
2000 * New unstructured in-message's blob content, with `->size() == ->capacity()`. We take ownership
2001 * of it (move it into the next layer); it shall be as-if default-cted on return.
2002 * @param sz
2003 * Number of bytes at `target_blob_ptr->begin()` that were read; the rest of `->size()` is garbage.
2004 * @param target_hndl
2005 * Native handle, if any, in the new unstructured in-message; we consume it (it ends up inside the
2006 * `Msg_in`, or auto-closes on any error return).
2007 * For certain compile-time properties of `Msg_in_pipe_t`, this must be `.get().null()`; for others
2008 * the reverse; and for others still it can be either. See Msg_in_pipe doc header.
2009 */
2010 template<typename Msg_in_pipe_t>
2011 void rcv_on_async_read_lead_msg(Msg_in_pipe_t* pipe, Segment_blob_in* target_blob_ptr, size_t sz,
2012 util::Own_native_handle&& target_hndl);
2013
2014 /**
2015 * Same as rcv_on_async_read_lead_msg() but for when `pipe->m_next_msg_lead_else_cont == false`.
2016 *
2017 * @note If we've tuned things appropriately, this should be invoked not too often, mostly
2018 * rcv_on_async_read_lead_msg(). With SHM-backing, this is never called.
2019 *
2020 * @param pipe
2021 * See rcv_on_async_read_lead_msg().
2022 * @param target_blob_ptr
2023 * See rcv_on_async_read_lead_msg().
2024 * @param sz
2025 * See rcv_on_async_read_lead_msg().
2026 * @param target_hndl
2027 * See rcv_on_async_read_lead_msg().
2028 */
2029 template<typename Msg_in_pipe_t>
2030 void rcv_on_async_read_continuation_msg(Msg_in_pipe_t* pipe, Segment_blob_in* target_blob_ptr, size_t sz,
2031 util::Own_native_handle&& target_hndl);
2032
2033 // start_and_poll() pipe: Main phase, structured-message layer.
2034
2035 /**
2036 * Once a structured in-message is completed, it is fed to this which processes it (the structured-message
2037 * layer proper).
2038 *
2039 * If and only #m_channel_err_code_or_ok is truthy on return, stop read chain; else continue it.
2040 * The former would occur if `msg_in` is broken somehow (other side didn't follow protocol/bug).
2041 *
2042 * @param msg_in
2043 * The completed structured in-message: after Msg_in::deserialize_mdt() but before
2044 * Msg_in::deserialize_body() (which may not be involved at all, if it's an internal message).
2045 */
2046 void rcv_struct_new_msg_in(Msg_in_ptr_uniq&& msg_in);
2047
2048 /**
2049 * Helper from `rcv_struct_new_msg_in()`: the case where the in-message has a sentinel message ID value, indicating
2050 * an internal message rather than one from a user send() (et al).
2051 *
2052 * If and only #m_channel_err_code_or_ok is truthy on return, stop read chain; else continue it.
2053 * The former would occur if `msg_in` is broken somehow (other side didn't follow protocol/bug).
2054 *
2055 * @param msg_in
2056 * See rcv_struct_new_msg_in(). Must have sentinel message ID.
2057 */
2058 void rcv_struct_new_internal_msg_in(const Msg_in_impl<Msg_in>& msg_in);
2059
2060 /**
2061 * Helper from `rcv_struct_new_msg_in()`: the case where #m_phase is Phase::S_CLI_LOG_IN, and the in-message has
2062 * the log-in-response value 1 + session-token=nil as required: Processes the in-message according to the rigid
2063 * log-in phase algorithm.
2064 *
2065 * If and only #m_channel_err_code_or_ok is truthy on return, stop read chain; else continue it.
2066 * The former would occur if `msg_in` is broken somehow (other side didn't follow protocol/bug).
2067 *
2068 * @param msg_in
2069 * See rcv_struct_new_msg_in(). Must have message ID 1 and session-token=nil.
2070 */
2071 void rcv_struct_new_msg_in_during_log_in_as_cli(Msg_in_ptr_uniq&& msg_in);
2072
2073 /**
2074 * Like rcv_struct_new_msg_in_during_log_in_as_cli() but for Phase::S_SRV_LOG_IN instead of CLI_LOG_IN.
2075 *
2076 * If and only #m_channel_err_code_or_ok is truthy on return, stop read chain; else continue it.
2077 * The former would occur if `msg_in` is broken somehow (other side didn't follow protocol/bug).
2078 *
2079 * @param msg_in
2080 * See rcv_struct_new_msg_in_during_log_in_as_cli().
2081 */
2082 void rcv_struct_new_msg_in_during_log_in_as_srv(Msg_in_ptr_uniq&& msg_in);
2083
2084 /**
2085 * Helper from `rcv_struct_new_msg_in()` (possibly indirectly): the case where the in-message's session-token
2086 * and message ID have been validated (and the latter indicates a user, not internal, message), and
2087 * the message ID (seq #) indicates this is the next expected in-order message (hence #m_rcv_msg_next_id was
2088 * just `++`ed). #m_phase may be any of the 3 values; but the special processing in
2089 * rcv_struct_new_msg_in_during_log_in_as_cli() or rcv_struct_new_msg_in_during_log_in_as_srv() must have
2090 * already completed if not LOGGED_IN.
2091 *
2092 * Assuming no detected error therein, this method processes taking `msg_in` from the lower 2-3 layers
2093 * (Channel-layer, structured message layer, possibly reassembly queue layer) into the next 1-2
2094 * (possibly caching in #m_rcv_pending_msgs, emission to user).
2095 *
2096 * Handles just `msg_in` itself: Does not check whether the gap to any messages in #m_rcv_reassembly_q
2097 * has been filled by this. That is, it's not self-perpetuating: caller must call us again for any
2098 * messages dequeued from #m_rcv_reassembly_q.
2099 *
2100 * If and only #m_channel_err_code_or_ok is truthy on return, stop read chain; else continue it.
2101 * The former would occur if `msg_in` is broken somehow (other side didn't follow protocol/bug).
2102 *
2103 * @param msg_in
2104 * See rcv_struct_new_msg_in().
2105 */
2106 void rcv_struct_new_msg_in_is_next_expected(Msg_in_ptr_uniq&& msg_in);
2107
2108 /**
2109 * Helper from rcv_struct_new_msg_in_is_next_expected() that reacts to receiving an otherwise valid
2110 * response in-message when no such response is expected. Hence it deals with
2111 * set_unexpected_response_handler() (if set) handler invocation and informing the opposing side, so that
2112 * it might invoke its set_remote_unexpected_response_handler() (if set) handler.
2113 *
2114 * @param msg_in
2115 * See rcv_struct_new_msg_in_is_next_expected().
2116 */
2117 void rcv_struct_inform_of_unexpected_response(Msg_in_ptr_uniq&& msg_in);
2118
2119 /**
2120 * Determines whether the given pipe should continue the async read chain (attempt to read at least one more
2121 * unstructured in-message). In and of themselves the question and the answer are simple; but before using
2122 * (and/or stopping to use) this helper please read doc header of Msg_in_pipe::m_gracefully_closed.
2123 *
2124 * @param pipe
2125 * Ref into #m_rcv_pipes array.
2126 * @return `true` <=> do not issue any more reads along `pipe`, as at least this specific pipe is hosed for
2127 * reading.
2128 */
2129 template<typename Msg_in_pipe_t>
2130 bool rcv_end_reads(const Msg_in_pipe_t& pipe) const;
2131
2132 // Registration.
2133
2134 /**
2135 * Core of expect_msg(), expect_msgs(), and expect_log_in_request(). Records the expectation of the given
2136 * message type (`which`) in #m_rcv_pending_msgs; then scans messages queued-up in #m_rcv_pending_msgs with matching
2137 * #Msg_which_in, in order. It async-emits one (if `one_off`) or all (otherwise) such messages into `*qd_msgs`
2138 * out-arg.
2139 *
2140 * Note that, if `one_off`, and a matching in-message is queued, #m_rcv_pending_msgs will not have changed
2141 * when comparing pre- and post-state.
2142 *
2143 * @param qd_msgs
2144 * See expect_msgs() and similar.
2145 * @param one_off
2146 * `true` for expect_msg() and expect_log_in_request() (which are almost identical); `false`
2147 * for expect_msgs(). In the latter case undo_expect_msgs() is a thing.
2148 * @param which
2149 * Message type to expect.
2150 * @param on_msg_func
2151 * See expect_msg() among others.
2152 * @return `true` usually; `false` if `which` expectation is already in #m_rcv_expecting_msg_map.
2153 * Corner case: if #m_phase is not LOGGED_IN (so SRV_LOG_IN, via expect_log_in_request()), and
2154 * #m_rcv_pending_msgs contains a queued-up in-message whose #Msg_which_in does not equal `which`:
2155 * the logging-in opposing peer disagrees with the expected protocol and issued a log-in request of
2156 * unexpected type; the channel is hosed, the on-error handler fires *synchronously* (see
2157 * expect_log_in_request() doc header), and `true` is returned (the operation ran and reported its
2158 * -- fatal -- result; `false` is reserved for no-op situations).
2159 */
2160 bool expect_msgs_impl(Msgs_in* qd_msgs, bool one_off, Msg_which_in which, On_msg_handler_ptr&& on_msg_func);
2161
2162 // Sending.
2163
2164 /**
2165 * send() and async_request() implementation.
2166 * Note this is still the higher-level, public send() or async_request() really;
2167 * it handles *user* messages; and once it has decided to indeed attempt the actual sending over
2168 * #Owned_channel, it synchronously invokes send_core(). To send an internal message use send_core()
2169 * directly.
2170 *
2171 * `check_unsendable(msg)` and `check_prior_error()` must have returned `true`.
2172 *
2173 * @param msg
2174 * See send() and sync_request().
2175 * @param originating_msg_or_null
2176 * See send() and sync_request().
2177 * @param err_code
2178 * Non-null target #Error_code.
2179 * @param on_rsp_func_or_null
2180 * For async_request() non-null pointer to `on_rsp_func`; else null.
2181 * @param id_unless_one_off
2182 * Ignored if `on_rsp_func_or_null` is null: See async_request().
2183 * @return See send() and async_request().
2184 */
2185 bool send_impl(Msg_out* msg, const Msg_in* originating_msg_or_null, Error_code* err_code,
2186 const On_msg_handler_ptr& on_rsp_func_or_null, msg_id_out_t* id_unless_one_off);
2187
2188 /**
2189 * Core of send() or internal-message-send: Given a list of raw blobs (intended as one per structured out-message)
2190 * sends them (first byte accompanied by the `Native_handle` supplied if any) out over the proper pipe.
2191 *
2192 * @see send_init_msgs(), the alternative to send_core() briefly used before the main phase (which uses send_core()).
2193 *
2194 * This is the last step of send() and async_request() (for user out-messages) or an internal attempt to send
2195 * internal out-message. As such (being the last step):
2196 * If user message (`msg` not null), and send_core() succeeds in Phase::S_SRV_LOG_IN, #m_phase moves to
2197 * Phase::S_LOGGED_IN within this method.
2198 *
2199 * @param blobs_out
2200 * 1+ messages, each as a blob, to send.
2201 * @param hndl
2202 * If not null, handle to send with `blobs_out.front()`.
2203 * @param err_code_or_ignore
2204 * See send_impl() (analogous meaning, even if send_impl() is not calling send_core() in this case).
2205 * Or, additionally, leave it null to ignore errors as follows:
2206 * #m_channel_err_code_or_ok is not touched even on error; the idea being this is a best-effort
2207 * internal message; and if it exposes error on an #m_channel out-pipe, then the next user send
2208 * will just see the same error and emit it that time. Otherwise an internal error could detect
2209 * the problem -- and our caller would not emit it. Thus it would get lost.
2210 * @return See send_impl() (analogous meaning, even if send_impl() is not calling send_core() in this case).
2211 * As of this writing, at this stage, there is only one remaining reason this might return `false`:
2212 * `Owned_channel::send*()` yielded transport::error::Code::S_SENDS_FINISHED_CANNOT_SEND.
2213 */
2214 bool send_core(const Segment_bufs& blobs_out, Native_handle hndl, Error_code* err_code_or_ignore);
2215
2216 /**
2217 * Essentially a much-cut-down version of send_core() that specifically sends, along all #Owned_channel pipes,
2218 * the `ProtocolNegotiation` and `ChannelHeader` messages -- the first payload required along each pipe. As of
2219 * this writing invoked from start_ops(), meaning before start_and_poll() or any send() or async_request().
2220 *
2221 * Post-condition: #m_init_msg_err_code_or_ok is falsy if there was no problem sending; else the error to emit
2222 * from subsequent start_and_poll() or send() or async_request() (whichever is called first).
2223 */
2224 void send_init_msgs();
2225
2226 // Utilities.
2227
2228 /**
2229 * Synchronously executes a user-facing handler of the given variety, right then and there: constructs a
2230 * `Handler_variety` from `members` and runs its `execute()`. We call such a call site a *handler-posting*:
2231 * the deliberate terminology marks it as a distinct, sensitive category of act (though nothing is queued
2232 * anywhere), subject to these simple but mandatory rules for any posting site:
2233 * - Post only once your own `*this` mutations for the triggering event are complete: the user handler may
2234 * re-enter public APIs (send(), expect_msgs(), create_msg()...) and must observe consistent state.
2235 * - Hold no iterator/reference into `*this` containers across the call (a re-entering API may mutate them).
2236 * - Post per completed event (each in-message individually; an error ASAP) rather than bunching executions
2237 * at the end of processing: steadier latency when one event-wait yields many in-messages.
2238 *
2239 * Why re-entrancy is otherwise fine: a handler cannot legitimately cause `(*on_active_ev_func)()` to run
2240 * (the user's event loop is mid-callback delivering the current event -- nor may they, per `sync_io`
2241 * contract), nor destroy `*this` (standard prohibition); and no public API reachable from a handler itself
2242 * posts (e.g., the send path reports errors via out-args and bare hose()) -- hence no recursion.
2243 *
2244 * The context for a posting is: we're processing an unstructured (low-level) message received along a pipe
2245 * of #Owned_channel; and it completed something such that the user
2246 * shall be informed of this via a completion handler they had registered. The relevant completion handler
2247 * varieties are 1-1 with the nested classes within our nested type Handlers.
2248 *
2249 * (async_end_sending() completion handler is a separate, lower-level thing.)
2250 *
2251 * @tparam Handler_variety
2252 * Specifies the variety of handler to invoke: a nested class of `struct` Handlers.
2253 * @param context
2254 * Brief context string for (immediate) logging.
2255 * @param members
2256 * Values for the `Handler_variety` object, describing the needed info. These are perfect-forwarded
2257 * into ctor of `Handler_variety`.
2258 */
2259 template<typename Handler_variety, typename... Members>
2260 void handlers_post(util::String_view context, Members&&... members);
2261
2262 /**
2263 * Helper for async handlers (immediately upon receiving a non-would-block result from lower-layer
2264 * `async_receive_*()`): returns `false` if and only if `err_code` indicates a new error
2265 * or #m_channel_err_code_or_ok indicates a previously-occurred one or both; in the former case *potentially*
2266 * does hose() (setting #m_channel_err_code_or_ok to `err_code`) + *potentially* sets
2267 * Msg_in_pipe::m_gracefully_closed to `true`. Logs appropriately.
2268 *
2269 * @see doc headers for #m_channel_err_code_or_ok and Msg_in_pipe::m_gracefully_closed.
2270 * In the thick of the state machine's logic, it's important to understand the hosed-status of `*this`
2271 * versus that of each `*pipe` (and our return value).
2272 *
2273 * @param pipe
2274 * Pointer into #m_rcv_pipes array.
2275 * @param err_code
2276 * Code from the async op.
2277 * @param context
2278 * Brief context string for logging.
2279 * @return In short: returns as-if `!rcv_end_reads(*pipe)`.
2280 * That is: `false` if `err_code` or a prior condition indicate the `*pipe` is hosed; `true` otherwise.
2281 * (Note that `false` here may or may *not* mean truthy #m_channel_err_code_or_ok.
2282 * Again: see Msg_in_pipe::m_gracefully_closed doc header.)
2283 */
2284 template<typename Msg_in_pipe_t>
2285 bool handle_async_err_code(Msg_in_pipe_t* pipe, const Error_code& err_code, util::String_view context);
2286
2287 /**
2288 * Helper that handles the situation where #m_channel_err_code_or_ok is falsy, and processing has
2289 * found a new error condition. Routes through hose() to set #m_channel_err_code_or_ok; then fires the
2290 * on-error handler (a handler-posting: see handlers_post()).
2291 *
2292 * Do *not* use when synchronously emitting an error (send_core() only as of this writing).
2293 *
2294 * @param err_code_not_ok
2295 * Truthy code (or assertion may trip).
2296 * @param context
2297 * Brief context string for logging.
2298 * @param lower_layer_originating
2299 * Forwarded to hose(); see its doc header. Default `false` covers nearly all call sites
2300 * (struc-protocol-layer detections); pass `true` from sites that promote a transport-layer
2301 * (Owned_channel) failure into a channel-hosing error.
2302 */
2303 void handle_new_error(const Error_code& err_code_not_ok, util::String_view context,
2304 bool lower_layer_originating = false);
2305
2306 /**
2307 * The single funnel for transitioning #m_channel_err_code_or_ok from falsy to truthy: assigns
2308 * `err_code_not_ok` to that member and logs final stats via log_stats(). All sites that hose the channel
2309 * must go through here.
2310 *
2311 * Caller is still responsible for any caller-specific WARNING and any subsequent on-error handler
2312 * work (e.g., handle_new_error() does the latter via handlers_post()).
2313 *
2314 * @param err_code_not_ok
2315 * Truthy code (or assertion may trip); the channel-hosing reason. Will be saved into
2316 * #m_channel_err_code_or_ok and never change thereafter.
2317 * @param context
2318 * For logging: the algorithmic context (function name or whatever).
2319 * @param lower_layer_originating
2320 * `true` if the cause is a transport-layer (#Owned_channel) failure -- in which case the
2321 * relevant sub-object will have hosed/logged its own stats already, so we do not re-log them.
2322 * `false` otherwise (our own layer's failures such as encountering wrong capnp protocol):
2323 * log_stats() additionally prints (still-healthy) Owned_channel sub-objects' stats as a snapshot
2324 * before they sit unused.
2325 */
2326 void hose(const Error_code& err_code_not_ok, util::String_view context, bool lower_layer_originating);
2327
2328 /**
2329 * INFO-logs current stats: the structured-channel-level #m_stats; and (conditionally) the
2330 * Owned_channel sub-objects' stats.
2331 *
2332 * Designed to be invoked in two situations: (1) clean dtor; (2) immediately upon hosing (via hose()).
2333 * In both cases there is a small budget (~1-2) of such prints per `*this` lifetime, so the INFO
2334 * log level is appropriate.
2335 *
2336 * Subtlety: Where called from a synchronous code path that may invoke a user handler immediately
2337 * thereafter, log this *before* invoking the handler -- to avoid the user re-entering us and
2338 * confusing the stats picture. hose() already does this.
2339 *
2340 * @param context
2341 * For logging: the algorithmic context (function name or whatever).
2342 * @param log_owned_channel_stats
2343 * If `true`, additionally print stats of the (1-2) Owned_channel sub-objects (snapshot at
2344 * struc-layer hosing time, when those sub-objects are still healthy). Pass `false` at
2345 * clean-dtor time (sub-objects will print themselves moments later via their own dtors)
2346 * and at lower-layer-originating hosing time (sub-objects already printed).
2347 */
2348 void log_stats(util::String_view context, bool log_owned_channel_stats) const;
2349
2350 /**
2351 * Helper that returns `false` if and only if start_ops() has not yet been called. This guard is required for
2352 * APIs that trigger #m_channel transmission API calls. Outgoing-direction such calls would be, e.g.,
2353 * send() and async_end_sending(). Incoming-direction transmission is all triggered by start_and_poll() (which
2354 * begins the async-read chain(s) indefinitely).

2367 * @param context
2368 * Brief context string for logging.

2371 bool check_prior_error(util::String_view context) const;

2373 /**
2374 * Helper for most public APIs to use at the top: ensures check_prior_error() passes, and that #m_phase equals

2380 * Brief context string for logging.

2383 bool check_phase_and_prior_error(Phase required_phase, util::String_view context) const;

2385 /**
2386 * send() and async_request() helper that returns `false` if and only if `msg` contains a native handle, but
2387 * #Owned_channel is compile-time-incapable of transporting them. No `*this` state other than
2388 * logging context is accessed.
2389 *
2390 * @param msg
2391 * See, e.g., send().
2392 * @return `false` if unsendable; else `true`.

2394 bool check_unsendable(const Msg_out& msg) const;
